# 🥞 Meerschaum Stack

Source: https://meerschaum.io/reference/stack/


# 🥞 Meerschaum Stack

The Stack uses [Docker Compose](https://docs.docker.com/compose/) to run a database, the API and console, Valkey, and Grafana together. Start it with `mrsm stack up -d`. See [upgrades and backups](upgrades.md) when maintaining an existing Stack.

## 🐳 Services

The default stack starts 4 services:

| Service | Description                                                                            | Image                                   |
|---------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| db      | TimescaleDB instance corresponding to `sql:main`.                                      | `timescale/timescaledb-ha:pg18`         |
| api     | Production Meerschaum Web API server corresponding to `api:main`.                      | `bmeares/meerschaum:<version>-full`     |
| valkey  | Valkey instance corresponding to `valkey:main`. Used for caching sessions in by `api`. | `valkey/valkey-bundle:latest`           |
| grafana | Grafana instance connected to `sql:main`.                                              | `grafana/grafana:latest`                |

You can edit the stack's Docker Compose file with `mrsm edit config stack`.

The `api` service runs the `full` image of the same release as the `mrsm` that writes the compose file (`bmeares/meerschaum:<version>-full`), so the API server and the client use the same version, and API plugins and the Dash console work without further installs. The image is built for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`.

??? info "Upgrading an existing stack to 5.x"
    Earlier versions of the stack ran `bmeares/meerschaum:api`. `mrsm stack` regenerates the compose file on every run: a root without `config/stack.yaml` takes the new image the next time you run `mrsm stack up -d`, which recreates only the `api` container (the volumes and the database are kept). After `pip install --upgrade meerschaum` the tag follows the new version in the same way, so run `mrsm stack up -d` after every upgrade (or `mrsm stack pull` first to fetch the image ahead of time).

    A `config/stack.yaml` that has a `docker-compose.yaml` section keeps its own `api` image, because the defaults only fill in what is missing. To move it, edit `services:api:image` with `mrsm edit config stack` to `bmeares/meerschaum:<version>-full` (or delete the `api` service's `image` line so the default applies), then run `mrsm stack up -d`. `mrsm stack config` prints the compose file that will run.

!!! tip "Entering the Meerschaum Docker image"
    Hop into a shell in the `api` service:

    ```bash
    mrsm stack exec -it api mrsm
    ```

### 🗄️ The Database Setup

<details markdown="1">
<summary>First-run setup, extensions, and health checks</summary>

The first time the `db` service starts on an empty volume, the image's entrypoint sets up the database. A new stack mounts Meerschaum's setup script as a single file into the image's own setup directory:

```yaml
volumes:
  - meerschaum_db_data:/home/postgres/pgdata
  - <root>/db/initdb/create-extensions.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/100_meerschaum.sql:z,ro
```

so the image's scripts run first and Meerschaum's runs last:

1. The image creates the `timescaledb` extension in the `postgres`, `template1` and `POSTGRES_DB` databases (new databases created from `template1` have it too).
2. `TIMESCALEDB_TELEMETRY: 'off'` (the stack default) turns off TimescaleDB's telemetry.
3. [`timescaledb-tune`](https://github.com/timescale/timescaledb-tune) tunes `postgresql.conf` for the container's memory and CPU limits. Set `NO_TS_TUNE: 'true'` in the service's `environment` to skip it (the stack's `command` still sets `max_connections` and `shared_buffers`, which win over the tuned values).
4. The image creates the `timescaledb_toolkit` extension.
5. `create-extensions.sql` creates `timescaledb`, `postgis`, `timescaledb_toolkit` and `pg_stat_statements` in `POSTGRES_DB`, each only when the image provides it (a `NOTICE` in the container's log names each one it skips, so another PostgreSQL image such as `postgres:18` or `postgis/postgis` still starts), and adds `pg_stat_statements` to `shared_preload_libraries` (keeping the entries already there) so its view can be queried once the server is up.

The `db` healthcheck asks the server over TCP (`pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5432 ...`, with a 300 second `start_period`): the entrypoint's setup server only listens on its Unix socket, so the service turns healthy (and `api` and `grafana` start) only after the setup is done. A passing check turns it healthy at once; the long start period only keeps a slow first setup (e.g. on a Raspberry Pi) from being reported unhealthy, which would abort `mrsm stack up`.

!!! note "The setup runs once"
    Docker runs the setup only when the data volume is empty. `mrsm stack` writes `create-extensions.sql` under your root directory once, when it is missing, and never overwrites it, so you may edit it before the first `mrsm stack up` (e.g. to create more extensions). Changing it later does nothing for an existing database: see [Upgrading the stack](/reference/stack/upgrades/) (`mrsm upgrade extensions`) for updating the extensions and settings of a database that already exists.

??? info "Stacks created before 5.0"
    Earlier versions mounted the whole `<root>/db/initdb` directory over `/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d`, which hid the image's own scripts (no telemetry opt-out, no tuning, no extensions in `template1`), and checked health over the Unix socket. `mrsm stack` regenerates the compose file on every run: a root without `config/stack.yaml` (v4's `mrsm stack` never writes one) takes the new defaults, and the next `mrsm stack up -d` recreates the `db` container once (the data volume is kept; extra scripts in `<root>/db/initdb/` are no longer mounted for a future fresh volume). A `stack.yaml` with a `docker-compose.yaml` section keeps that section as it is. See the [migration guide](/reference/migrating-to-v5/#deployment).

</details>

### Docker Images

Choose a variant of [`bmeares/meerschaum`](https://hub.docker.com/r/bmeares/meerschaum):

| Tag | Included | Best suited to |
|---|---|---|
| `full` / `latest` | Native CLI, Python SDK and all extras (including Dash/API), Cargo, rustc, C/C++ build tools, pip, Git and interactive tools | First-time users and plugin development |
| `rust` | Native CLI, core API/MCP, database connectors and runtime libraries; no Python or compilers | Small native deployments and prebuilt Rust plugins |
| `rust-full` | Everything in `rust`, plus Cargo, rustc, Git and native build tools; no Python | Building Rust source plugins without a Python installation |
| `slim` / `minimal` | Python and the base wheel; no optional extras or Rust toolchain | Small Python installations where dependencies are supplied separately |
| `api` | Deprecated alias of `full` | Existing deployments |

Every variant runs the same Rust engine and uses the same configuration and plugin formats.
The Dash console and Python plugins require a Python variant. A `.rs` source plugin needs
Cargo for its first build and after edits; use `rust-full` or `full`, or ship a prebuilt plugin
with `rust`. The toolchain variants also cache the base dependencies for single-file Rust plugins,
so a minimal Rust plugin can build offline. Additional plugin dependencies use normal Cargo
downloads. Native-only deployments never need a Python host. Mount `/home/meerschaum/.cargo`
when you want dependency downloads to persist across `rust-full` or `full` containers.

Pin a version with `{version}-{variant}`, for example `5.0.1-rust` or
`5.0.1-full`. Releases publish `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64` and update the floating tags;
pre-releases publish only version-qualified tags, for `linux/amd64`.
`{version}-api` continues to alias `{version}-full`.

Build locally with `docker buildx build --target rust --load -t mrsm:rust .` (replace
`rust` with `rust-full`, `slim`, or `full`). A plain `docker build .` produces `full`.
`full` intentionally has a larger size budget because it includes both language toolchains.
Native drivers may still require vendor libraries, such as Oracle Instant Client.

Containers are upgraded by pulling the desired image and recreating the service, preserving
the mounted Meerschaum root. `mrsm upgrade mrsm` inside a container reports this ownership
rather than changing packages in the running image.

## 🗒️ Requirements

You need [Docker](https://www.docker.com/get-started) installed to run the stack. To install Docker, follow [this guide](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/) or do the following:

=== "Windows / MacOS"
    Install [Docker Desktop](https://www.docker.com/get-started).

=== "Linux"
    Search your repositories for `docker.io` or run this script:

    ```bash
    curl https://get.docker.com | sh
    ```

    Don't forget to add yourself to the `docker` user group and log out and back in.

    ```bash
    sudo usermod -aG docker myusername
    ```


## 🟢 Starting the Stack

Run the following command to bring up a database and Grafana:

```bash
mrsm stack up -d db grafana
```

<asciinema-player src="/assets/casts/stack.cast" autoplay="true" loop="true" size="small" preload="true" rows="10"></asciinema-player>

!!! note ""
    The `stack` command is a wrapper around a pre-configured [`docker-compose`](https://docs.docker.com/compose/) project. Don't worry if you don't have `docker-compose` installed; in case it's missing, Meerschaum will automatically install it within a virtual environment for its own use.

    Refer to the [`docker-compose` overview page](https://docs.docker.com/compose/reference/overview/) to see the available `stack` commands.

<img src="/assets/screenshots/grafana-dashboard.png" alt="Example Grafana Dashboard" width="85%" style="display: block; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">

!!!info ""
    Grafana is included in the Meerschaum stack, pre-configured with the Meerschaum TimescaleDB database.

    Open a web browser and navigate to [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000) where you can log into Grafana with username `admin`, password `admin`.

### Built-in performance dashboards

The Stack provisions three dashboards in Grafana's **Meerschaum Dashboards** folder:

- **Meerschaum Performance**, the overall duration, failure, and write-rate picture.
- **Pipe Performance**, focus on one Pipe and its recent syncs.
- **Pipeline Performance**, compare Pipeline runs and follow their results.

Use them to find slow Pipes, inspect recent failures, and follow P95 duration, retries, chunks, and **rows affected/s**. Replacements count deleted plus new rows; unchanged syncs affect zero rows.

Grafana queries the configured database directly with its data-source credentials. Its visibility follows those database permissions. The web console and HTTP API apply their Pipe and team access rules. See [Sync metrics](../api-instance/sync-metrics.md) for capture and history limits.

## 💾 Backing Up and Upgrading the Database

`mrsm backup postgres` takes an online backup of the stack's database (nothing is stopped) into
`<root>/backups/postgres/<timestamp>/`, and `mrsm restore postgres` puts a backup into a new volume
and switches the stack to it, keeping the current one. `mrsm upgrade postgres` moves the database
to a newer PostgreSQL major the same way (a backup first, then a verified restore). See
[Backing up and restoring](/reference/stack/upgrades/#backing-up-and-restoring) and
[Upgrading PostgreSQL](/reference/stack/upgrades/#upgrading-postgresql).

## 🛑 Stopping the Stack

If you want to stop all the services in the stack, run the stack command with `down`:

```bash
mrsm stack down
```

To remove all services in the stack and delete all data, use the `-v` flag:

```bash
mrsm stack down -v
```

<asciinema-player src="/assets/casts/stack-down.cast" autoplay="true" loop="true" size="small" preload="true" rows="12"></asciinema-player>

!!! warning "Data Loss Warning"
    The `-v` flag in `stack down -v` will delete ALL volumes in the stack. That includes pipes' data!

    To delete a specific service's volume, run the command `docker volume rm`, e.g. to delete just Grafana's data:
    ```bash
    docker volume rm mrsm_grafana_storage
    ```

## 📝 Editing the Stack

Certain parameters like the main database username and password are linked from the [connectors](/reference/connectors/) configuration, which may be accessed with `mrsm edit config`.

You can find the complete [Docker Compose](https://docs.docker.com/compose/) YAML file with:

```bash
mrsm edit config stack
```

# Upgrades and backups

Source: https://meerschaum.io/reference/stack/upgrades/

# ⬆️ Upgrading the Stack

Pulling newer images (`mrsm stack pull`, or `mrsm upgrade mrsm`) updates the stack's software, but
not everything inside its database volume. This page covers what an upgrade leaves behind and the
commands that finish the job. See [the stack page](index.md) for how the stack's database is set
up in the first place.

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Update extension versions in an existing database | `mrsm upgrade extensions` |
| Move the Stack database to a newer PostgreSQL major | `mrsm upgrade postgres` |
| Make an online backup | `mrsm backup postgres` |
| Restore into a new volume | `mrsm restore postgres` |

## Updating extensions

Run `mrsm upgrade extensions` to preview and approve updates. Long-running clients must reconnect afterward. Database restart settings are shown separately.

<details markdown="1">
<summary>Extension plans, permissions, and restart behavior</summary>

### What lags and why

Docker runs the database's setup scripts (`/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d`) only when the volume is
empty, so after a new image is pulled the database keeps the **extension versions it was created
with**. The image ships the new versions (and, for TimescaleDB, the older libraries too, so
nothing breaks), but the database keeps using the old ones until each extension is updated:

- **TimescaleDB** keeps loading its old library (fixes and features of the new release stay off).
- **PostGIS** (with `postgis_raster`, `postgis_topology`, ...) keeps its old SQL functions.
- **TimescaleDB Toolkit** and any other extension keep their old SQL objects.

Meerschaum tells you when this happens: `mrsm stack up` and `mrsm start api` print a one-line
hint when an extension of the instance is older than the server's version, and
`mrsm upgrade mrsm` offers the update after it brings the stack back up. `mrsm doctor` reports it
too.

The stack's own setup has also missed a few settings on stacks created before 5.0: the compose
file's `TIMESCALEDB_TELEMETRY: 'off'` never applied (the image's setup script that reads it was
hidden by the stack's mount), and `pg_stat_statements` was created without being added to
`shared_preload_libraries`, so its view cannot be read.

### The command

```bash
mrsm upgrade extensions
```

It reads the instance's database (`-i` picks another instance; the default is the configured
instance, usually `sql:main`), prints a plan and asks before changing anything:

```text
┏━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ Database   ┃ Extension           ┃ Installed ┃ Available ┃ Statement                                       ┃
┡━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│ meerschaum │ timescaledb         │ 2.29.2    │ 2.30.2    │ ALTER EXTENSION timescaledb UPDATE;             │
├────────────┼─────────────────────┼───────────┼───────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ meerschaum │ timescaledb_toolkit │ 1.22.0    │ 1.26.0    │ ALTER EXTENSION "timescaledb_toolkit" UPDATE;   │
└────────────┴─────────────────────┴───────────┴───────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

| Flag / word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-i, --instance` | The PostgreSQL instance to update (e.g. `sql:main`). A non-PostgreSQL instance has nothing to update. |
| `<database> ...` | Other databases on the same server to update as well, e.g. `mrsm upgrade extensions template1 postgres`. Databases are never updated unless they are the instance's own or named here: a shared server may host other applications' databases. |
| `-y`, `-f` | Update without asking, including the `pg_stat_statements` preload on the stack's database (see below). |
| `--noask` | Accept the default answers: yes for the extensions, no for the `pg_stat_statements` preload (the statement is printed instead). |

### What it changes

Each update runs in a **new session of its own, as that session's first statement**:

| Extension | Statement |
|---|---|
| `timescaledb` | `ALTER EXTENSION timescaledb UPDATE;` (TimescaleDB refuses the update in a session that has already loaded the old library, so nothing else runs before it.) |
| `postgis`, `postgis_raster`, `postgis_topology`, `postgis_sfcgal`, `postgis_tiger_geocoder` | `SELECT postgis_extensions_upgrade();` (one call updates the family.) |
| anything else (`timescaledb_toolkit`, `pg_stat_statements`, ...) | `ALTER EXTENSION "<name>" UPDATE;` |

An extension the server cannot update (no update path from the installed version, e.g. a version
newer than the image's) is reported and skipped.

On **the stack's own database**, connected as a superuser, it also does the following. The
instance is the stack's database when it is `sql:main`, the stack was set up from this Meerschaum
root (its Compose origin labels identify this root's compose file), and the running `db`
container's initialized database and published or internal port match the connector. A read-only
check also matches PostgreSQL's system identifier and server address to that container, then
proves that the container can see a uniquely named live probe connection. This also separates
cloned clusters on different Docker hosts. A `sql:main` override to another localhost port or database is treated as an explicit instance:
extensions can still be updated there, while stack-specific settings and restarts are omitted.
The API and Grafana containers must also belong to this root before they can be restarted.

- applies the stack's `TIMESCALEDB_TELEMETRY: 'off'` the way the image's setup script does:
  `ALTER SYSTEM SET timescaledb.telemetry_level = 'off'`, `SELECT pg_reload_conf()`, and
  unscheduling TimescaleDB's telemetry job in each updated database;
- asks (a separate question, default no) whether to add `pg_stat_statements` to
  `shared_preload_libraries` with `ALTER SYSTEM`, keeping the libraries already listed. `-y` and
  `-f` add it without asking (so does `mrsm upgrade mrsm -y` when it runs the update); `--noask`
  keeps the default answer and prints the statement instead. It takes effect after the database
  restarts: `mrsm stack restart db`. Meerschaum never restarts the database for you.

The result counts the extensions updated, failed and skipped.

### Permissions

Updating an extension needs a superuser or the extension's owner (the stack's `sql:main` user is
a superuser). When an update is refused, the others still run and the result names the exact
statement to run as a superuser, connected to that database, e.g.:

```bash
psql -d meerschaum -X -c 'ALTER EXTENSION timescaledb UPDATE;'
```

(`-X` keeps `psql` from running a startup file first; TimescaleDB's update must be the session's
first statement.)

### Restarts

Sessions that loaded the old TimescaleDB library keep it until they reconnect. After a
TimescaleDB update on the stack's database, `mrsm upgrade extensions` restarts the stack's `api`
and `grafana` services if they are running (their pooled sessions hold the old library). Restart any other long-running process that uses the database (jobs,
API servers on other hosts) so it loads the new version:

```bash
mrsm restart jobs
```

</details>

## Upgrading PostgreSQL

Run `mrsm upgrade postgres` for a planned dump-and-restore into a new volume. The old volume is kept. Read the downtime and rollback details before approving a production upgrade.

<details markdown="1">
<summary>Upgrade workflow, downtime, verification, and rollback</summary>

The image of the stack's `db` service decides its PostgreSQL major. A stack whose `stack.yaml`
names the image keeps that major (stacks set up by Meerschaum 3.0 to 3.3 with a `stack.yaml` run
`timescale/timescaledb-ha:pg17`, new stacks get `pg18`). A new major cannot read an older major's
data directory, and the stack's images ship one PostgreSQL major each, so moving to a new major is
a dump and a restore. `mrsm upgrade postgres` does it, the way TimescaleDB requires, and never
touches the old data: you can go back at any time.

### The command

```bash
mrsm upgrade postgres                                  # to the default stack image's major
mrsm upgrade postgres 18                               # to a major, in the same image family
mrsm upgrade postgres timescale/timescaledb-ha:pg18    # to an image
mrsm upgrade postgres rollback                         # back to the old database
```

A major keeps the image family and variant of the current image:

| Current image | With `18` |
|---|---|
| `timescale/timescaledb-ha:pg17` (also `-oss`, `-all`) | `timescale/timescaledb-ha:pg18` |
| `timescale/timescaledb:latest-pg16` (also `-oss`) | `timescale/timescaledb:latest-pg18` |
| `postgres:17` (also `-alpine`, ...) | `postgres:18` |
| `postgis/postgis:17-3.5` | `postgis/postgis:18-3.5` |

Any other image, or a pinned tag (`pg17.5-ts2.20.3`, `postgres:17.6`), cannot be mapped: name the
target image, or follow [the manual procedure](#the-manual-procedure).

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-y, --yes` | Answer yes to the questions (pulling the image, starting the upgrade). |
| `-f, --force` | Like `--yes`, and go on although other clients are connected or disk space is low. |
| `--noask` | Take each question's default: nothing is pulled and the upgrade does not start. |
| `--debug` | Print the Docker commands; keep the new volume of a failed run for inspection. |

### What it does

Nothing changes until the plan is shown and confirmed:

1. **Preflight** (read-only). The stack's `db` service must be running. The command reads its
   server, databases, extensions and data volume, pulls the target image (after asking), and
   starts a throwaway container of it to check that it can create every extension, and every
   database's exact TimescaleDB version. It checks the free space for the backup and for Docker's
   volumes, and lists what may write to the database: the stack's services that depend on `db`
   (`api`, `grafana`, ...), other connected clients and the Meerschaum jobs running in this root.
2. **Quiesce.** The services that depend on `db` are stopped; `db` runs through the dump. If any other
   client is still connected, the upgrade stops here (unless `--force`): what it would write
   after the dump would not be in the new database. The old database is disconnected from its
   Docker networks before dumping, blocking new external TCP clients through the final checks
   and its stop; its loopback and Unix socket remain available to the dump tools. Network aliases
   and declared static addresses are recorded before disconnecting, and restored after it stops
   or during recovery. TimescaleDB's background jobs are paused until the old server restarts.
   Stop writers running inside the database container or using its Unix socket too: these
   administrative connections are outside the external-client fence.
3. **A full backup first**, exactly as [`mrsm backup postgres`](#backing-up-and-restoring) takes
   it, into `<root>/backups/postgres/<UTC timestamp>/`, with the new image's client tools (as
   PostgreSQL recommends) when they can reach the old server, and with the exact row count of
   every table recorded in each dump's own snapshot. After all dumps, connected clients, per-table
   write counters and structure are checked again. Any write after a snapshot aborts the upgrade,
   including an update that leaves the row count unchanged. Then the old database stops, before
   the restore begins. Stop external writers before starting; `--force` permits connected clients
   but does not bypass detected changes. Host/shared network namespaces and unsupported custom
   network attachments cannot be fenced; without `--force` they are refused. With `--force` the
   command's warnings explicitly describe the risk of concurrent writes being lost. Enabled logical
   replication subscriptions and unhandled background workers are also refused unless forced.
   A source running as a standby is always refused.
4. **Restore into a new volume.** A new volume, `<volume>_pg<major>` (e.g.
   `mrsm_meerschaum_db_data_pg18`, or a run-specific name if that name is in use), is set up by
   the new image in a temporary container with the stack's environment, command and setup script; it has no network and no published port, so
   nothing else can write to it. Then, per database: TimescaleDB is created at **the dump's
   version** (TimescaleDB restores only into the same version), the roles and the data are
   restored between `timescaledb_pre_restore()` and `timescaledb_post_restore()` with
   `--exit-on-error` (the restore list skips only the extensions that already exist, so every
   remaining error is real), then the database's own settings and `ANALYZE`. The server settings
   made with `ALTER SYSTEM` (`postgresql.auto.conf`, e.g. TimescaleDB's telemetry level or
   `shared_preload_libraries`) are carried over, and the temporary server is restarted to prove it
   still starts with them. If the old server's TimescaleDB is too old for the new image, it is
   updated on the old server first (the plan says so).
5. **Verify.** The copy must match the recorded counts and structure exactly. Its extensions are
   then updated to the new image's versions (TimescaleDB as the first statement of its own
   session, PostGIS with `postgis_extensions_upgrade()`), then its structure is checked again.
   Any difference stops the upgrade: nothing is switched, the stopped services start again, and the new volume is removed.
6. **Switch.** With the old `db` already stopped, `stack.yaml` is copied byte for byte into the backup's
   directory, and only three things in it change: the `db` image, its data volume entry and that
   volume's declaration under `volumes:`. Block-style YAML keeps its comments and formatting;
   if a safe line edit is unavailable (for example flow-style YAML or anchors), the plan says
   that the config will be rewritten. The original remains in the backup. If there was no stack
   config file, the command creates one with the current full stack config, pinning its defaults.
   The compose file is regenerated, `db` starts on the new volume, and the services that were running start again.

The old volume is never removed and nothing writes to it but its own server (and, only when the
plan says so, the TimescaleDB update of step 4).

On Linux and macOS, Ctrl-C, SIGTERM and a closed terminal (SIGHUP) stop the running step and
put the old stack back. Further signals are ignored during cleanup. On Windows a second Ctrl-C
exits immediately. Run long upgrades in tmux or screen. A forced kill or power loss can interrupt
cleanup: the next upgrade or restore detects the run and offers to put it back first;
`mrsm upgrade postgres rollback` also recovers an interrupted run. An interrupted rollback is
completed on its requested old volume, keeping both database volumes. Backups only warn about
unfinished recovery. A command that changes the stack waits (up to two minutes) for a
`docker compose` command of the project that a killed run left running, before it reads the
stack or puts it back. A `restore postgres` that began with the stack's `db` stopped leaves it
stopped when it is put back (a stopped database is never started on a volume the plan promised not
to modify).

If the disk of `<root>/backups/postgres` fills up, a failed upgrade removes its own dump files so
that its end can still be recorded (the stack is put back either way, and the result says so);
free space and run it again.

### Downtime

The services that use the database (the API, Grafana) are down from the start of the backup to the
end of the switch. External database connections are unavailable from network isolation before
the dump through the switch; the database process itself stops at the end of the dump. The whole run takes about as long as one dump, one restore and two passes of row counts: a few seconds for a small
database, tens of minutes for a large one. Stop the Meerschaum jobs and other clients that write
to the database before you start (`mrsm stop jobs`), and start them again afterwards.

While an upgrade, a restore or a rollback moves the database, `mrsm stack up`, `mrsm stack start`
and `mrsm stack restart` of that stack are refused (a stopped old `db`, or a service that uses it,
would write to the database being copied, and those writes would not be in the copy). Wait for the
command to finish; `--force` bypasses the check. If the old `db` is started again anyway, the
command notices before it switches, stops with "The old database ran again", puts the stack back
and removes the new volume: nothing is lost, and you run it again once the clients are stopped. A
backup only reads the database and never holds these commands back.

### Rollback and cleaning up

`mrsm upgrade postgres rollback` (after its own plan and question) stops the stack's database and
the services that use it, puts `stack.yaml` back from the latest upgrade's (or restore's) copy
(the current one is kept next to it as `stack.yaml.before-rollback-<timestamp>`), and starts `db`
on the old volume with the old image again. **What was written to the database after the upgrade
is not in the old volume.** The new volume is kept.

The roles and their passwords come with the data. After a rollback (or a `restore postgres` of an
older backup) a password changed since then is the old one again, so the stack's services cannot
log in until the role and the stack config agree. The command tries the stack's own login when it
is done and says so when the server refuses it; set the role's password to the configured one
(`ALTER ROLE ... PASSWORD ...`) or put the old password back in the config. If you edited
`stack.yaml` after the upgrade (a port, a password, another service), the plan warns that the
rollback puts the file from before the upgrade back, and the result names the copy of your
current file: `stack.yaml.before-rollback-<timestamp>` next to the upgrade's backup.

When you are satisfied with the new database, free the space of the old one, with the names the
upgrade printed:

```bash
docker volume rm mrsm_meerschaum_db_data                  # the old volume
rm -r ~/.config/meerschaum/backups/postgres/<timestamp>   # its backup (Linux; `<root>/backups/...`)
```

After a rollback, the new volume is kept too. A later upgrade chooses another unused name; it
never reuses or removes an existing volume automatically.

### When it refuses

- The stack's `db` is not running (`mrsm stack up -d db` first), or its container runs another
  image than the stack config says. When its image cannot start on the data (the stack config's
  image moved to a newer major while the data stayed, e.g. a stack without `stack.yaml` that
  follows a new default image), the command reads the data's major from the volume and says
  which image to pin first (`mrsm edit config stack`), so that the data runs again and can then be
  upgraded.
- The stack config is patched by `MRSM_CONFIG`, `MRSM_PATCH` or a patch directory (the edit of
  `stack.yaml` would not take effect), or an override file changes the `db` image or volume.
- The data is in a bind mount, not a named volume; or the server has tablespaces outside its data
  directory; or a database is a template or does not allow connections.
- An extension, or a database's TimescaleDB version, cannot be created by the new image.
- A database's encoding or locale cannot be recreated by the new image; additional named
  volumes, mounts inside a data directory or over a socket directory, or volume `driver` /
  `driver_opts` would require a manual migration.
- Another root uses the same Compose project: the container's Compose labels must identify this
  root's stack file. Commands lock both the root and the project on the Docker daemon.
- PostgreSQL older than 13.

The settings in the old volume's `postgresql.conf` and `pg_hba.conf` are not copied (the new image
writes its own); settings made with `ALTER SYSTEM` are, except preloaded libraries the new image
does not have (a warning names them). File paths, socket / port settings, archiving, recovery and
replication settings are not carried to the temporary server; the plan and warnings identify
these. Bind mounts outside the data and socket directories are read-only in that server.

### The manual procedure

For a database that is not the stack's (another server, a bind mount, a custom image), the same
steps by hand: `pg_dump` from the old server, `pg_restore` into a new one of the new major, with
TimescaleDB at the same version on both sides. Use the client tools of the **new** version, and
stop every client that writes to the database first. With the old server at `old`, the new one at
`new`, and one database `mydb`:

```bash
export PGUSER=mrsm PGPASSWORD=...    # a superuser of both servers

# 1. The database's TimescaleDB version on the old server (here 2.29.2). The new server must
#    be able to create it: SELECT version FROM pg_available_extension_versions WHERE name = 'timescaledb'
psql -h old -d mydb -X -At -c "SELECT extversion FROM pg_extension WHERE extname = 'timescaledb'"

# 2. The roles and the database.
pg_dumpall -h old --globals-only -f globals.sql
pg_dump -h old -Fc --create -d mydb -f mydb.dump

# 3. The roles ("role ... already exists" for the new server's own superuser is expected).
psql -h new -d postgres -X -f globals.sql

# 4. The database, and TimescaleDB at the SAME version as in the old database.
# Use the dump's DATABASE entries to keep its owner, encoding, locale and database settings.
pg_restore -l mydb.dump | awk '/^[0-9]+; [0-9]+ [0-9]+ (DATABASE - |DATABASE PROPERTIES - |COMMENT - DATABASE |ACL - DATABASE |SECURITY LABEL - DATABASE )/' > mydb-create.list
pg_restore -h new -d postgres --create --exit-on-error -L mydb-create.list mydb.dump
psql -h new -d mydb -X -c "CREATE EXTENSION timescaledb VERSION '2.29.2'"

# 5. Everything but the extension that now exists, between the pre- and post-restore calls.
pg_restore -l mydb.dump | grep -v -E '(EXTENSION - |COMMENT - EXTENSION )timescaledb *$|^[0-9]+; [0-9]+ [0-9]+ (DATABASE - |DATABASE PROPERTIES - |COMMENT - DATABASE |ACL - DATABASE |SECURITY LABEL - DATABASE )' > mydb.list
psql -h new -d mydb -X -c "SELECT timescaledb_pre_restore()"
pg_restore -h new -d mydb --exit-on-error -L mydb.list mydb.dump
psql -h new -d mydb -X -c "SELECT timescaledb_post_restore()"
psql -h new -d mydb -X -c "ANALYZE"

# 6. TimescaleDB's update to the new server's version: the first statement of its own session.
psql -h new -d mydb -X -c "ALTER EXTENSION timescaledb UPDATE"
```

Then compare the row counts and database settings on both servers. Repeat steps 1, 2 and 4 to 6
for each database. In a Docker setup, run these commands in a container of the new image that can
reach both servers, and point the service at the new server's volume when it matches.

</details>

## Backing up and restoring

`mrsm backup postgres` runs online. `mrsm restore postgres` verifies a backup and restores into a new volume. Writes made since the backup stay in the previous volume.

<details markdown="1">
<summary>Backup files, retention, restore checks, and rollback</summary>

### `mrsm backup postgres`

An **online** backup of the stack's database: nothing is stopped or restarted, and clients keep
writing. Each database is dumped from one consistent snapshot (`pg_dump -Fc` of a snapshot that a
session exports for it, compressed with zstd when the server's `pg_dump` supports it), together
with the roles (`pg_dumpall --globals-only`), and the database's structure and a row estimate are
recorded in the same snapshot.

```bash
mrsm backup postgres
```

Each backup is a directory `<root>/backups/postgres/<UTC timestamp>/`:

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `globals.sql` | The roles (`pg_dumpall --globals-only`; it holds their password hashes). |
| `NN-<database>.dump` | Each database (`pg_dump -Fc --create`; readable with `pg_restore`). |
| `manifest.json` | The PostgreSQL version and image, each database's extensions and their versions (TimescaleDB's above all: a restore needs it), each file's size and SHA-256, and row estimates. |

The files are written to `<timestamp>.partial/` and the directory is renamed once every dump has
been read back with `pg_restore --list`; a failed backup removes it. The directories are readable
by you only on Linux and macOS (0700 directories, 0600 files); Windows uses the directory's
inherited access controls. The free disk space is checked first (`--force`
goes on anyway). The command prints the path, the sizes and the time it took.

Backups contain the roles and each connectable, non-template database. They do not copy
`postgresql.conf`, `pg_hba.conf`, or customizations of `template1`; keep those separately.
Settings made with `ALTER SYSTEM` are recorded, subject to the restore exclusions above.

**Scheduled backups.** The command asks nothing, so it runs as a [job](../background-jobs/index.md):

```bash
mrsm backup postgres -s 'daily' -d
```

**Retention.** Every backup is kept unless you set how many to keep, e.g. with
`mrsm edit config system`:

```yaml
backups:
  postgres:
    keep: 7
```

After each successful backup, the oldest complete backups beyond that number are removed. Only
directories whose manifest says they are complete backups are removed: never an upgrade's or a
restore's directory, nor anything else in `backups/postgres/`.

### `mrsm restore postgres`

```bash
mrsm restore postgres                     # the newest complete backup
mrsm restore postgres 20261018T120000Z    # a backup by its timestamp (an upgrade's backup works too)
mrsm restore postgres /path/to/backup     # a backup directory elsewhere
mrsm restore postgres rollback            # back to the database before the restore
```

The restore never overwrites the current database. Every file is first checked against the size
and SHA-256 in the backup's manifest (damage is refused before anything changes;
these checksums do not authenticate the backup or protect against someone editing both files
and manifest), and a throwaway container of the stack's image checks that it can read every dump and
create every extension and TimescaleDB version. After the plan and its question (`--yes` answers
it), the backup is restored the way an upgrade restores its dump: into a NEW volume, in a temporary
container without network, verified against the manifest (each database's tables, hypertables,
compression settings, chunks, policies and extensions), and only then is the stack's `db` switched
to it (`stack.yaml` is copied first; only the `db` volume changes). The services that use the
database are stopped only for the switch, and the database keeps running until then.

**Everything written since the backup is not in the restored database**: it stays in the previous
volume, which is kept. `mrsm restore postgres rollback` (or `mrsm upgrade postgres rollback`)
switches back to it; remove it with `docker volume rm` once you no longer need it.

A backup of an older PostgreSQL major is restored into the stack's (newer) image the way an upgrade
does it; a backup of a newer major than the image is refused (set an image of that major for `db`
first).

Before `mrsm stack up`, a PostgreSQL image whose major can be identified is checked against
`PG_VERSION` in existing named volumes through a read-only mount, without pulling an image.
A mismatch refuses startup and explains how to pin the old image and run `mrsm upgrade postgres`.
A database already running its configured image skips the check. `mrsm stack up --force` bypasses
it; Compose does not receive that flag. `mrsm stack start` and `mrsm stack restart` start the
containers that exist with the image they were created from, so they skip this check; they, like
`stack up`, wait for an upgrade, restore or rollback that is moving the database (see
[Downtime](#downtime)). Unknown image families and tags such as `latest` cannot
be checked this way.

</details>

# 🌐 API Instance

Source: https://meerschaum.io/reference/api-instance/

# 🌐 API Instance

The Meerschaum API instance (and [Web Console](/get-started/start-api/)) lets you manage [pipes](/reference/pipes/), [jobs](/reference/background-jobs/), and [connectors](/reference/connectors/) over the Internet. Start the API server with the [stack](/reference/stack/) or via `start api`; see [Deployment](#deployment) below for ways to run Meerschaum in production.

## Usage

Starting the Meerschaum API server lets you treat your host as the following:

- [API instance](/reference/connectors/#instances-and-repositories)
  For managing pipes.
- [Plugin repository](/reference/plugins/repositories/)
  For storing plugins.
- [Remote executor](/reference/background-jobs/executors/)
  For running jobs.

### Adding Connectors

Add new `api` connectors with `bootstrap connector` or declaring an [environment connector](/reference/connectors/#environment-connectors):

```bash
# URI is in the form 'protocol://user:pass@host:port'
export MRSM_API_FOO='https://foo:bar@mrsm.example.com'
```

### Remote Actions

Add `-e` to client commands to [execute them remotely](/reference/background-jobs/executors/) on your API instance:

```
sync pipes -e api:main
```

When running the `mrsm` shell, the `executor` command allows you to temporarily run all the commands in your session remotely (like the `instance` command):

```
executor api:main
```

### API Documentation

You can visit your API instance's Swagger documentation by navigating to `/docs` or `/redoc`. Every route is listed there with the scopes it needs. Saved Pipelines, their runs and the console's actions have routes of their own, which answer `{"success": ..., "message": ..., ...}` with real status codes: see [Pipelines, Runs and Actions over HTTP](/reference/api-instance/routes/).

### Permissions and Rate Limits

Which routes a server serves, who may run actions and how often a client may call are settings under `api:permissions`: see [Permissions and Rate Limits](/reference/api-instance/permissions/). To publish only plugin routes and plugin pages (a public dashboard), use the [public preset](/reference/api-instance/permissions/#the-public-preset):

```
mrsm start api --public
```

## Deployment

It's common in production deployments to stand up a public-facing API instance. See below for deployment tips:

On a new instance, the first account becomes an administrator. Create that account before opening the instance to visitors. Self-registration then closes unless you set `api:permissions:registration:users: true`. New users are Editors by default: they may work with pipes, but actions and the web terminal need the Operator role (`actions:execute` and `webterm:use`). Administrators manage users, roles and teams in the console's **Users & Teams** page.

`mrsm start api --secure` restricts actions and terminals to administrators; `--private` requires authentication on every endpoint. Enabling registration with Operator as the default role lets any visitor register and open a shell on this server. See [roles, teams and permissions](/reference/api-instance/permissions/#roles-and-teams) and [HTTPS](#tls-ssl-https).

### Meerschaum Stack (easiest)

If you have [Docker](https://www.docker.com/get-started/) installed, the most straightforward way to deploy is via the [Meerschaum stack](/reference/stack/):

```
mrsm stack up -d
```

This starts an internally-managed, pre-configured Docker Compose project with an `api` service that runs on [http://localhost:8000](http://localhost:8000).

The environment in the `api` service is updated such that [connectors](/reference/connectors/) from your host are passed to the container.

!!! tip "Want to manage Docker yourself?"
    You can run the [`bmeares/meerschaum` Docker image](https://hub.docker.com/r/bmeares/meerschaum) if you'd like to add Meerschaum to another Docker Compose project. You may also edit the `stack` Docker Compose project with `mrsm edit config stack` under the key `docker-compose.yaml`.

### Bare Metal

If you don't want to deploy with Docker, you can run an API instance on your host directly:

!!! note inline end ""
    The `--production` flag stops serving the interactive API docs (`/docs`, `/redoc`) unless `api:endpoints:docs_in_production` is set.

```
mrsm start api --production
```

For example, this is a common pattern for [standing up a `systemd` service](/reference/background-jobs/) to start the API server:

```
mrsm start api --production --name api-instance -d
```

### TLS / SSL / HTTPS

Give `start api` a private key and its certificate, and the API server speaks HTTPS itself (HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1):

```bash
mrsm start api --production \
  --keyfile /etc/meerschaum/tls/privkey.pem \
  --certfile /etc/meerschaum/tls/fullchain.pem
```

Or set the files in the config (`mrsm edit config api`), so every `start api` (and the background job of `start api -d`) uses them:

```yaml
api:
  server:
    ssl_keyfile: /etc/meerschaum/tls/privkey.pem
    ssl_certfile: /etc/meerschaum/tls/fullchain.pem
```

The server prints where it serves, for example `Serving HTTPS on https://mrsm.example.com:8000 (certificate for mrsm.example.com, valid until 2027-01-25).` Without a key and a certificate it speaks plain HTTP, as always.

- **The files** are PEM. The key may be unencrypted PKCS#8, PKCS#1 (RSA) or SEC1 (EC). The certificate file holds the server's certificate first, then its intermediates, as Let's Encrypt's `fullchain.pem` does. `start api` checks both before it starts and stops with the reason when something is off: a key without a certificate (or the reverse), a file it cannot read, swapped files, a key that does not belong to the certificate.
- **Renewals need no restart.** The server reads both files again every 30 seconds and on `SIGHUP` (`kill -HUP <pid>`), and new connections get the renewed certificate. When the new files do not load yet (a renewal caught between writing the key and the certificate), it keeps serving the previous certificate and says why if the problem persists. (So with HTTPS, `SIGHUP` reloads instead of stopping the server: stop it with Ctrl-C, `SIGTERM` or `mrsm stop jobs`.)
- **Plain HTTP on the HTTPS port** gets `/healthcheck` answered, so container healthchecks such as `curl --fail http://localhost:8000/healthcheck` keep working, and a redirect to `https://` for everything else.
- **Clients.** Point `api` connectors at the server with `https`, e.g. `MRSM_API_MAIN='https://user:pass@mrsm.example.com:8000'` or `protocol: https`. For a self-signed certificate, add its CA to the client's trust store, or set `verify: false` on the connector (no certificate check: for testing only).
- **The web console, the web terminal and MCP** work over HTTPS unchanged. The server's own callers on the same machine (the console's Python host, jobs that install plugins from this server) reach it through a separate plain-HTTP listener on `127.0.0.1` with a random port, which is never exposed.

!!! tip "Let's Encrypt"
    Let's Encrypt's private keys are readable only by root. Rather than running the API as root, copy the files where the server's user can read them whenever they are renewed, with a deploy hook (here for the user `meerschaum`):

    ```bash
    sudo mkdir -p /etc/meerschaum/tls
    sudo certbot certonly --standalone -d mrsm.example.com --deploy-hook \
      'install -m 640 -g meerschaum "$RENEWED_LINEAGE/privkey.pem" "$RENEWED_LINEAGE/fullchain.pem" /etc/meerschaum/tls/'
    ```

    The server picks up each renewal by itself. Ports below 1024 (such as 443) need privileges on Linux: serve on a higher port (`-p 8443`) or forward 443 to it.

In the [stack](/reference/stack/), mount the certificate directory into the `api` service (`mrsm edit config stack`, under `docker-compose.yaml`) and set `api:server:ssl_keyfile` / `ssl_certfile` to the paths inside the container; its healthcheck needs no change.

The 4.1 keys `api:uvicorn:ssl_keyfile` and `api:uvicorn:ssl_certfile` still work (with a notice to move them to `api:server`). `--keyfile '' --certfile ''` serves plain HTTP even when the config sets a key and a certificate.

A reverse proxy that terminates TLS, such as Caddy or NGINX, remains a fine choice, for example to serve several sites on port 443: see the [example NGINX configuration](/reference/api-instance/nginx/). Behind a proxy, set `api:server:forwarded_allow_ips` and `api:server:proxy_headers` so that the server sees each client's address (see [Permissions](/reference/api-instance/permissions/)).

### Docker

If you're building your own Docker images, consider basing off the [`bmeares/meerschaum` Docker image](https://hub.docker.com/r/bmeares/meerschaum), as is done in the [`mrsm compose` template repository](https://github.com/bmeares/mrsm-compose-template/blob/main/docker/Dockerfile):

```docker
FROM bmeares/meerschaum

COPY --chown=meerschaum:meerschaum ./ /app
WORKDIR /app
RUN mrsm compose init

ENTRYPOINT ["/app/docker/bootstrap.sh"]
```

This image comes pre-installed with common database drivers and package dependencies. Note this image is configured to run as a non-privileged user `meerschaum`.

Of course, you can always `pip install` Meerschaum into your own custom image:

```docker
FROM python

# Install dependencies into the virtual environment:
RUN pip install meerschaum && mrsm upgrade packages api -y

# or to install dependencies globally:
# RUN pip install meerschaum[api]

ENTRYPOINT ["python", "-m", "meerschaum"]
```

### AWS

Run the [`bmeares/meerschaum` Docker image](https://hub.docker.com/r/bmeares/meerschaum) with ECS or on an EC2 like you would any other Docker container. See the [Docker section above](#docker) if you want to build your own images.

### Helm Chart (k8s)

If you are running Kubernetes, consider the [Meerschaum Helm chart on Artifact Hub](https://artifacthub.io/packages/helm/meerschaum/meerschaum). It's configured to run the [`bmeares/meerschaum` Docker Image](https://hub.docker.com/r/bmeares/meerschaum) for k8s environments.

# Security and Tokens

Source: https://meerschaum.io/reference/api-instance/tokens/

# 🪙 Tokens

Meerschaum tokens are long-lived API keys that grant programmatic access to a Meerschaum instance. They are a secure way to authenticate for services like IoT devices or CI/CD pipelines without using your username and password.

Tokens are tied to a specific user and have a defined set of permissions, called **scopes**.

When you create a token, you receive three key pieces of information: a Client ID, a Client Secret, and an API Key.

!!! warning "Write it down!"
    The Client Secret is **only shown once** upon token creation, so be sure to copy it somewhere safe when registering tokens.

- **Client ID:** A public, unique identifier (`UUID`)
- **Client Secret:** A private secret (treat this like a password)
- **API Key:** To be used in the `Authorization` header (contains Client ID and Secret within).

Additionally, tokens have the following attributes:

- **Label:** A human-readable name to help you identify the token
- **Expiration:** An optional timestamp after which the token will become invalid
  Set the `expiration` to `None` to prevent a token from expiring (use at your own risk!)
- **Scopes:** A list of permissions that define what actions the token can perform
- **User:** The user account that owns the token

---

## ➕ Registering

You can create new tokens via the action `register token`:

```bash
mrsm register token
```

This will prompt you for the owner of the token and print the Client ID, Client Secret and API Key. Registering to an `api` instance will assign the token the connector's configured user.

## 🌐 Web UI

The easiest way to can manage tokens is on the [Web Console](/reference/api-instance/web-console). Open the user menu (your username, at the top right) and choose **Tokens**. From here, you can:

-   Create new tokens with **New token**.
-   Edit, invalidate, or delete existing tokens from the context menu (`⠇`).

When you create a new token, a form prompts you for a label, expiration date, and scopes. The **Grant all scopes, including custom and future ones** switch (the scope `*`) is on by default for an administrator or a holder of `*` (for anyone else the form starts from your own scopes and the switch is off); turn it off to pick built-in scopes from a checklist and to type custom (plugin) scopes. The edit form of a token that holds `*` shows the switch on, and saving it keeps `*`. After registration, you **must** copy the generated credentials, as the secret will not be shown again.

<img src="/assets/screenshots/web-console-tokens.png" alt="Web Console tokens page">

---
## 🐍 Python API

In addition to the CLI and Web UI, you can manage tokens directly on [instance connectors](/reference/connectors/instance-connectors/).

### Creating a Token

To create a token, instantiate a `meerschaum.core.Token` object and call its `register()` method.

??? example "Creating a new token"
    ```python
    import meerschaum as mrsm
    from meerschaum.core import Token, User

    # Tokens must be associated with a user.
    user = User('myuser', instance='sql:main')

    # The token will be managed by the 'sql:main' instance connector.
    token = Token(
        label='my-iot-device',
        user=user,
        instance='sql:main',
    )

    # The register() method generates the credentials and saves the token.
    success, msg = token.register()
    if not success:
        print(msg)
    else:
        print(f"Successfully registered token '{token.label}'")
        print(f"  Client ID: {token.id}")
        print(f"  Client Secret: {token.secret}")
        print(f"  API Key: {token.get_api_key()}")
    ```

### Fetching Tokens

You can retrieve a list of all tokens for a user from an instance connector.

```python
import meerschaum as mrsm

conn = mrsm.get_connector('sql:main')
user = mrsm.core.User('myuser', instance=conn)

# Admins can see all tokens, including those without a user.
# Regular users only see their own tokens.
tokens = conn.get_tokens(user=user)

for token in tokens:
    print(token)
```

### Editing a Token

You can modify a token's label, expiration date, and scopes.

```python
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

# Get the first token from the list.
token = tokens[0]

# Extend the expiration by 30 days.
if token.expiration:
    token.expiration += timedelta(days=30)
else:
    token.expiration = datetime.now(timezone.utc) + timedelta(days=30)

# Limit the token's scopes.
token.scopes = ['read:pipes', 'write:pipes']

success, msg = token.edit()
```

### Invalidating and Deleting Tokens

If a token is compromised, you can invalidate it immediately. Invalidated tokens cannot be used but remains registered; deleting a token removes it permanently.

```python
# Invalidate the token.
success, msg = token.invalidate()

# Delete the token permanently.
success, msg = token.delete()
```

---

## ⚙️ Authorization

There are two ways to use a token to authenticate with the API:

1. Post the **Client ID** and **Client Secret** to `/login`.
  The standard OAuth flow now accepts `client_id` and `client_secret` (in addition to `username` and `password`). This returns short-lived bearer tokens.
2. Set the **API Key** directly in the `Authorization` header.
  For situations where the standard OAuth flow isn't feasible (e.g. some IoT workloads), you can directly embed the API Key in the `Authorization` header. The API Key wraps the Client ID and Secret and is authenticated on every request.

??? example "Authenticating with `curl`"

    ```bash
    # Replace <API_KEY> with your generated key.
    export API_KEY="mrsm-key:YTg1ZTI3NDEtZ..."

    curl -X GET http://localhost:8000/pipes \
      -H "Authorization: $API_KEY"
    ```

---

## 🎯 Scopes

A token (and a user, through the `scopes` attribute of their account) holds a list of scope strings, and every API route requires the scopes it names (`pipes:read`, `jobs:execute`, `jobs:stop`, ...). A request missing one is refused with `403` and `Missing required scope: '<scope>'`.

- **`*` grants all scopes, including custom and future scopes.** It is stored literally and checked on every request, so a `*` token keeps working when a plugin defines a new scope or a later release adds one. Use it for trusted automation. `edit tokens` and `edit users` keep a `*` you type as `*` (v4 replaced it with the list of built-in scopes), and so do `register tokens --scopes '*'`, `POST /tokens/register` with `"scopes": ["*"]` and the console's token form. When no scopes are given, a new token gets its owner's scopes, and a new user (`register users`) follows the instance's default role (see [Teams, Access and Locks](../actions/teams-and-access.md)).
- **A token carries at most its owner's scopes.** Registering or editing a token with a scope the owner does not hold, or with `*` when the owner is neither an administrator nor a holder of `*`, is refused with `403` (or a failure in `register tokens` / `edit tokens` and the console) naming each disallowed scope; nothing is trimmed. A token registered without scopes gets its owner's own, and editing a token keeps the scopes it already holds. The console's register form starts from your own scopes, and "Grant all scopes" is on by default only for an administrator or a holder of `*`.
- **Only the owner or an administrator may change a token.** Editing, invalidating or deleting another user's token answers `403`; only an administrator may make an invalidated token valid again; an edit that omits `scopes` or `is_valid` keeps them. `mrsm edit tokens` and the other token actions work on the instance directly with the operator's own access and are trusted; the rule is enforced by an `api:` instance's server.
- **Custom scopes are plain strings.** A plugin's `@api_plugin` routes may require any scope, for example `ScopedAuth(['myplugin:read'])`, and a token is granted it by listing it explicitly (`--scopes myplugin:read pipes:read`). Meerschaum does not validate scope names, so a typo grants nothing.
- **Stopping a job needs `jobs:execute` and `jobs:stop`.** v4 required a misspelled `josb:stop` that no one could hold, so only `*` tokens and administrators could stop jobs over the API. v5 requires `jobs:stop`, and still accepts a token that explicitly holds the legacy `josb:stop` in its place.
- **Running actions.** Remote actions need `actions:execute` and `jobs:execute`; creating jobs also needs `jobs:write`. Setting `api.permissions.actions.non_admin: false` (`start api --secure`) restricts these operations to administrators. Restricted keys follow the remote command limits even when their owner is an administrator. Pipe Sync and Verify controls use the Pipe's own permissions. See [who may run actions](/reference/api-instance/permissions/#who-may-run-actions).

```bash
mrsm register tokens --name automation --scopes '*'
mrsm register tokens --name plugin-reader --scopes myplugin:read pipes:read
```


---

# Permissions and Rate Limits

Source: https://meerschaum.io/reference/api-instance/permissions/

# 🛡️ Permissions and Rate Limits

An API server decides three things about every request: whether the route is served at all (route groups), who may call it (authentication and [scopes](/reference/api-instance/tokens/#scopes)), and how often (rate limits). All of it lives under `api:permissions` in your config (`mrsm edit config api`).

## Route groups

Every route belongs to a group, and a group that is not served answers `404` (it is not proxied to plugins either, so a plugin cannot serve a core path you turned off).

| Group | Routes |
|---|---|
| `pipes` | `/pipes/*` and `/metadata` |
| `pipelines` | `/pipelines` and `/pipelines/*` (saved Pipelines) |
| `engine` | `/engine/*` (engine state, run history, run event streams) |
| `actions` | `/actions/*` and `/execute*` (running actions) |
| `jobs` | `/jobs/*` and `/logs/*` |
| `connectors` | `/connectors` |
| `users`, `tokens`, `plugins` | `/users/*` and `/teams/*`, `/tokens/*`, `/plugins/*` |
| `version` | `/version`, `/version/mrsm` |
| `misc` | `/healthcheck`, `/info`, `/chaining`, `/favicon.ico` (and `/id` with `--debug`) |
| `index` | `/` (a redirect to the console or the docs) |
| `mcp` | `/mcp` ([MCP server](/reference/mcp/)) |
| `dash` | the web console's own pages (the Python API host reads it) |

`/login` is always served unless you disable it explicitly. The API docs (`/docs`, `/redoc`, `/openapi.json`), the web terminal and plugin routes are not core groups.

A request's group is decided on its decoded path, the path the API host would serve: `/%64ocs` is `/docs` and `/my%2Dplugin/data` is `/my-plugin/data`, for the allowlist, the public preset and rate limits alike.

```yaml
api:
  permissions:
    routes:
      ### Glob patterns of the groups to serve (missing or null: every group).
      allowlist: ['*']
      ### Groups to turn off, whatever the allowlist says (`login` too).
      disabled: ['actions']
```

## The public preset

For a server whose job is to publish plugin routes and plugin pages to anyone (a public dashboard, a data feed), the public preset turns everything else off:

```yaml
api:
  permissions:
    preset: public
```

or, for one run, `mrsm start api --public`.

It serves only `/login`, `/healthcheck`, `/version`, `@api_plugin` routes, plugin pages (and the console's login page, for plugin pages that require a login) and the static files they need. The web console's own pages, the web terminal, `/actions`, `/execute`, user registration, the API docs (`/docs`, `/redoc`, `/openapi.json`) and every other core route group are off. The server says so at startup:

```text
Public preset: serving only /login, /healthcheck, /version, plugin routes and plugin pages; ...
```

Your explicit route settings still apply on top of the preset. A group the allowlist names (any pattern but the default `*`) is served too, and `disabled` still turns groups off:

```yaml
api:
  permissions:
    preset: public
    routes:
      ### Also serve the pipe routes (for `api:` connectors syncing into this server) and the docs.
      allowlist: ['pipes', 'docs']
      ### No version endpoint either.
      disabled: ['version']
```

## Roles and teams

The first account on an empty instance is an administrator, even when user registration is off. After that, only administrators create accounts unless you turn on `api:permissions:registration:users` (default `false`). A self-registered account joins **Everyone** and receives the default role, set with `api:permissions:default_role` (`editor` by default).

| Role | Permissions |
|---|---|
| **Viewer** | Read visible pipes, Pipelines, runs, jobs, logs, plugins and the connectors list; manage their own account and tokens. |
| **Editor** | Viewer, plus register, define, edit and sync pipes, read SQL, and start existing jobs. |
| **Operator** | Editor, plus execute actions, open the web terminal and create, stop, pause or delete jobs. |
| **Admin** | Every permission, user and team administration, and connector details (user type `admin`). |

An administrator may set a role or an explicit permission list for a user. Explicit permissions replace the role; an empty list grants no permissions. A token's scopes are intersected with its owner's current permissions, so reducing the user's rights also reduces existing tokens. Lists made before the new scopes existed keep their earlier meanings: `pipes:write` also registers and defines pipes, and `actions:execute` also opens the terminal. New lists can use `pipes:register`, `pipes:define_sql` and `webterm:use` independently. See [token scopes](/reference/api-instance/tokens/#scopes).

Every user belongs to the built-in team **Everyone**, which cannot be left, renamed or deleted. Administrators create additional teams, appoint managers and choose memberships. Managers add and remove members of their own teams and manage those teams' pipe access. A user's primary team supplies the team for the pipes and jobs they create. Renaming a team updates its pipes and jobs; deleting it moves them to Everyone.

Pipes without access settings belong to Everyone and remain shared. A pipe's `access` parameters choose its owner, team, visibility (**team**, **private**, or **everyone**) and who may edit it (**team** or **owner**). Only its owner, team managers and administrators may change its access or locks. The server stamps new pipes with the caller as owner; a caller cannot impersonate another owner when registering. [Pipe access and locks](/reference/pipes/access-and-locks/) describes the settings and Python API.

The HTTP API, MCP and console enforce these rights and filter hidden members from Pipelines, runs, events, lineage and searches. Jobs started through them belong to their creator and primary team; local jobs belong to Everyone. Email addresses are visible to their owners, administrators, and managers of a team the user belongs to. Local SQL / Valkey credentials are the trust boundary: direct CLI and Python access with them sees everything. Pipe locks apply everywhere, including local access, and no force flag bypasses them.

A connector's `teams: [Data, Operations]` attribute restricts who may use it through the API. Setting SQL definitions requires `pipes:define_sql`; the server refuses internal tables and the tables of pipes the caller cannot see, before and after templates resolve. These SQL checks are best effort. True isolation needs separate connectors and database users with appropriate database permissions.

## Who may run actions

Actions need `actions:execute` and the terminal needs `webterm:use` (Operator and administrators by default). Pipe Sync and Verify controls need `pipes:write` and edit rights on each selected pipe; they do not require arbitrary action execution. Pipeline sync checks every member it would change; a sync-locked member is skipped using its existing data. Remote action selections may not include pipes the caller cannot see or change.

Remote actions run on this server. Nonadministrators cannot redirect them to another executor or inspect server configuration with `show connectors`; use the console's Connectors page for the details your account may see. For Pipe registration and sensitive parameter edits, use the console or dedicated Pipe endpoints. Restricted API keys keep these limits even when their owner is an administrator.

`api:permissions:actions:non_admin: false` (`start api --secure`) further restricts actions, terminals and console mutations to administrators. Meerschaum 4's explicit `actions:non_admin: true` maps the default role to Operator for compatibility, unless `default_role` is set explicitly. The shipped configuration leaves that compatibility key unset and uses Editor.

## Permissions fail closed

When the server cannot read a user's permissions, teams or credentials, it refuses the request with `503` and asks to try again. It never treats a failed read as a default permission grant. Password login fails the same way. Identities are cached for at most five seconds and pipe access for three seconds; changes through this server clear those caches immediately. This holds for every instance type (SQL, Valkey, `api:` and custom instance connectors). Local `register tokens` and `edit tokens` refuse without changing anything when they cannot read the owner's permissions.

## Rate limits

Rate limits are token buckets per client and route group: `requests` per `seconds`.

```yaml
api:
  permissions:
    rate_limits:
      login: {requests: 10, seconds: 60}
      ### `max` and `window_seconds` are accepted too.
      pipes: {max: 1000, window_seconds: 60}
      ### A path prefix limits a plugin's routes (here `/my-plugin` and everything under it).
      /my-plugin: {requests: 30, seconds: 60}
      ### A glob over the groups: every other group.
      '*': {requests: 600, seconds: 60}
```

- A key is a route group (the table above, plus `login`, `docs`, `mcp`, `webterm` and `other` for anything else, such as plugin routes), a glob pattern over them (`'*'`, `'pipe*'`), or a path prefix starting with `/`.
- A path prefix matches the path itself and everything below it (`/my-plugin` covers `/my-plugin/data`, not `/my-plugins`), compared with the decoded path (`/my%2Dplugin/data` counts too); the longest prefix wins and all the paths under it share one bucket per client. Otherwise the first matching group pattern applies, with a bucket per group.
- Without `seconds`, the window is one minute.
- A limited request gets `429` with `Retry-After`.
- An entry the server cannot use (a count below 1, a window that is not a positive number, a key it does not know inside an entry, a name that matches no route group) is reported at startup, naming the entry, and the rest of the config still applies.

The client is the connection's address, or behind a trusted proxy (`api:server:forwarded_allow_ips`, `api:server:proxy_headers`) the first untrusted `X-Forwarded-For` address.


---

# Pipelines, Access and Actions over HTTP

Source: https://meerschaum.io/reference/api-instance/routes/

# 🛣️ Pipelines, Access and Actions over HTTP

Besides the existing pipe, user, token, plugin and job routes, an API server has routes for saved [Pipelines](/reference/pipelines/), their runs, [teams and pipe access](/reference/pipes/access-and-locks/) and the console's background actions. Existing route bodies remain compatible; the access model also filters and authorizes those routes. Your server lists them all, with their scopes, at `/docs`.

## One response shape

The routes under `/pipelines`, `/engine`, `/execute` and `/teams`, and the new user-permission and pipe-access routes below, answer with a JSON object that says whether the request succeeded and what happened, plus the data:

```json
{"success": true, "message": "Found 2 runs.", "runs": [...]}
```

```json
{"success": false, "message": "Pipeline 'daily' is not registered on 'sql:main'."}
```

The status code tells the kind of failure: `400` (the request is invalid; a list of `errors` comes with it when there are several), `401` (not logged in), `403` (not allowed), `404` (not found), `409` (a conflict: it already exists, a lease is held, a scheduled job uses it), `429` (rate limited), `500` (the server failed), `501` (this server cannot do it). A `500`'s message names what failed only for administrators; everyone else gets a generic message, and the details are in the server's log.

## Saved Pipelines

| Route | Scopes | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /pipelines` | `pipes:read` | The saved Pipelines (`pipelines`, their definitions) |
| `GET /pipelines/{name}` | `pipes:read` | One Pipeline: `pipeline` (its definition), `members` (each target pipe, and whether it is registered) and `last_run` |
| `POST /pipelines/{name}/plan` | `pipes:read` | What a run would do: `plan`, `text` (the plan table) and `warnings`. Nothing moves and nothing is registered |
| `POST /pipelines/{name}/sync` | `pipes:write`, `jobs:execute` | Start a run in the background: `run_id`, `job`, `stream`, `log_stream`, `logs` |
| `POST /pipelines/{name}/rename` | `pipes:read`, `pipes:write`, `pipes:register`, `pipes:delete` | Rename a live registration, keeping its identity and access |

Each takes `?instance_keys=` for a Pipeline saved on another instance. `plan` and `sync` take an optional body with the window (`{"begin": "2026-01-01", "end": "2026-02-01"}`, ISO datetimes or integers); `sync` also takes a `run_id` of your own.

```bash
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://mrsm.example.com/pipelines/daily/sync
```

```json
{
  "success": true,
  "message": "Started Pipeline 'daily' (run '2026-10-27T05-00-00Z-api-1a2b3c4d5e6f') as job 'execute-1a2b3c4d'.",
  "run_id": "2026-10-27T05-00-00Z-api-1a2b3c4d5e6f",
  "job": "execute-1a2b3c4d",
  "stream": "/engine/runs/2026-10-27T05-00-00Z-api-1a2b3c4d5e6f/events/stream?wait=30",
  "log_stream": "/logs/execute-1a2b3c4d/stream",
  "logs": "/logs/execute-1a2b3c4d"
}
```

The run is a background job, as when you press Sync on the console's Pipelines page: `stream` follows its events ([Following a run over HTTP](/reference/pipelines/visualization/#following-a-run-over-http)) and `GET /engine/runs/{run_id}` reads it when it is done. The caller needs the listed permissions and edit rights on every member the run will change; a sync-locked member is skipped using its existing data. Each instance the Pipeline touches must be allowed. `--secure` further restricts remote mutations to administrators.

The registration routes the CLI and Python SDK use to save definitions are also here: `GET /pipelines/keys`, `POST /pipelines/{name}/register` (`409` if it exists), `PATCH /pipelines/{name}/edit`, `DELETE /pipelines/{name}/delete` (`409` while a scheduled job runs it), `GET /pipelines/{name}/id` and `/attributes` (`404` if it is not registered), and the leases of `/pipelines/leases`. A Pipeline named `keys` or `leases` is reachable through those routes but not through `GET /pipelines/{name}`.

The server assigns each new Pipeline registration a fresh ID. Edits and authorized renames keep a current ID; unproven legacy identities are upgraded. The SDK uses the authoritative saved definition.

??? example "Rename a Pipeline"
    Send `{"new_name": "evening"}` to `POST /pipelines/daily/rename`. Add `expected_revision` or `expected_id` to reject a stale request. The response includes the saved `pipeline`. An occupied destination, changed source, lock or referencing job refuses the move.

## Runs

| Route | Scopes | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /engine/runs` | `pipes:read` | Runs, newest first (`runs`) |
| `GET /engine/runs/{run_id}` | `pipes:read` | One run (`run`) and each pipe's result (`nodes`) |
| `GET /engine/runs/{run_id}/events/stream` | `pipes:read` | A run's events as Server-Sent Events |
| `POST /engine/run-generations` | `pipes:read` | Check whether retained runs match current registrations and access |

`GET /engine/runs` filters with:

- `pipeline`: the runs of a saved Pipeline;
- `pipe`: the runs that synced a pipe, as a pipe reference (`sql:main|sql:main|weather|None`);
- `status`: `success`, `failed` or `running`;
- `since`: runs started at or after an ISO datetime;
- `limit`: at most this many (default 100, at most 1000);
- `run_id`: that run and its pipes' rows;
- `instance_keys`: the instance that keeps the history (default the server's).

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "https://mrsm.example.com/engine/runs?pipeline=daily&status=failed&since=2026-10-01"
```

The other `/engine/*` routes carry the engine's own state for `api:` instances ([Engine State](/reference/pipelines/state/)): reads need `pipes:read`, writes `pipes:write`.

??? info "Registration checks for API-backed tools"
    Send at most 256 run IDs to `POST /engine/run-generations`:

    ```json
    {"run_ids": ["daily-2026-10-27T05-00-00Z-1a2b3c4d"]}
    ```

    The response's `generations` maps each requested ID to `true` or `false`. Hidden, missing, stale or unproven history returns `false`. Registration checks also apply to administrator credentials; stored registration evidence is never returned. Checks use the API credential's access; a hosted tool must also enforce its visitor's access.

## Console actions

`POST /execute` runs an action line (`{"sysargs": ["sync", "pipes", "-c", "sql:main"]}`) as a temporary background job owned by the caller and answers with `job`, `sysargs`, `stream` (`/logs/{job}/stream`) and `logs` (`/logs/{job}`). `stream` is `null` when the server does not serve the log stream (`--no-dash`, or the `jobs` route group is off), and `logs` too without the `jobs` group. It needs `actions:execute`, `jobs:execute` and `jobs:write`; a user who is not an administrator runs only what the console offers (`GET /execute/policy`). `POST /execute/validate` answers whether the caller may run a line in the web terminal, `GET /execute/runs` lists the retained summaries of finished runs, and `POST /execute/runs/{name}/retain` keeps one as a persistent job.

## Jobs

Every job the server starts (`POST /jobs/{name}`, `POST /execute`, `POST /pipelines/{name}/sync`) records its caller as `owner` and the caller's primary team as `team`, whatever the request says. `/jobs/*`, `/logs/*` and the log stream show a job only to the people who may see it: its team, its owner and administrators (a console run: its owner, its team's managers and administrators; a job created on the server's host: everyone); to anyone else it does not exist (`404`). See [Who Sees a Job](/reference/background-jobs/access/) for the permissions each operation needs.

## Teams, permissions and pipe access

| Route | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GET /teams`, `GET /teams/{name}` | List teams or read a team's members and managers; `?counts=true` includes affected pipe/job counts. |
| `POST /teams/{name}/register` | Create a team (admin). |
| `PATCH /teams/{name}/edit` | Edit members; admins also edit managers and attributes. A team manager may edit their own team's members. |
| `POST /teams/{name}/rename`, `DELETE /teams/{name}/delete` | Rename or delete a team and update its pipes and jobs (admin). |
| `GET /users/permissions`, `GET /users/{username}/permissions` | Read role, effective permissions, teams and primary team; email visibility follows the caller. |
| `PATCH /users/{username}/permissions` | Update role or explicit permissions (admin), or permitted own attributes. |
| `GET /pipes/{connector}/{metric}/{location}/access` | Read a visible pipe's access, locks and the caller's allowed operations. |
| `PATCH /pipes/{connector}/{metric}/{location}/access` | Update owner, team, visibility or edit mode. |
| `POST /pipes/{connector}/{metric}/{location}/lock`, `POST .../unlock` | Set or remove the named locks, e.g. `{"locks": ["sync", "drop"]}`. |

Pipe access and lock changes require the owner, a manager of the pipe's team, or an admin, together with the relevant permissions. Only an admin may assign another owner. Hidden objects answer `404`; an operation refused by a lock answers `409`. Team and permission routes belong to the `users` route group; pipe access belongs to `pipes`. See [Roles and teams](permissions.md#roles-and-teams) for the permission rules.

## Row counts

`GET /pipes/{connector}/{metric}/{location}/rowcount` (a Meerschaum 4 route) also takes `estimate=true`, for the database's estimate of the table's size (its statistics, without counting) where it keeps one, and the exact count otherwise; and `params` as a JSON query string (`?params={"station":"KGMU"}`) for clients that cannot send a body with a `GET`.
