Any of these may be wrapped in `Result` (an `Err` is reported as the executor's failure).
`LogEvent` is `Lines(Vec<String>)`, `Timeout` or `End(Option<SuccessTuple>)`; the closure may
block up to the timeout it receives, and it is dropped when the host stops following.
`show logs` follows a job through `monitor_logs`; an executor without it shows its logs only
with `show logs --nopretty`, which reads `get_logs`.

### Streaming connectors

`fn subscribe` inside a `#[make_connector]` module makes the connector type a stream source
for `sync pipes --listen` and the engine's supervised streams, the counterpart of an
`IS_STREAMING` connector's `subscribe`. A top-level `fn subscribe` does the same for
`plugin:<name>`. `subscribe` may take `pipe: &Pipe` (with its
[host calls](#talking-to-meerschaum), while the stream opens), `connector: &Connector` and `kwargs: &Value` (the sync's
keyword arguments, as Python's `subscribe` receives them) and returns, optionally in a
`Result`, a closure `impl FnMut(Duration) -> Batch` (or `-> Result<Batch>`), an
`impl Subscription`, a `Box<dyn Subscription>` (the Cargo SDK's type), or a type the file
implements `Subscription` for. A function named `subscribe` with other parameters or another
return type is an ordinary helper, at the top level and in a connector module, as it was
before streaming connectors (a connector module whose only function is such a `subscribe`
is an error that says why).

```rust
/// Readings as they arrive.
#[make_connector]
mod ticker {
    fn subscribe(pipe: &Pipe, kwargs: &Value) -> Result<impl FnMut(Duration) -> Batch> {
        let station = pipe.parameters()["fetch"]["station"].as_str().unwrap_or("a").to_owned();
        let mut next = 0;
        // Inside `Ok(...)`, Rust needs the closure's parameter type spelled out.
        Ok(move |timeout: Duration| {
            std::thread::sleep(timeout.min(Duration::from_secs(1)));
            next += 1;
            Batch::RowsAck(vec![json!({"id": next, "station": station})], next)
        })
    }

    // Optional: the tokens of batches whose rows committed.
    fn ack(tokens: &[u64]) -> Result<()> {
        Ok(())
    }
}
```

The host calls the closure for each batch, with the longest time it may block, and only
after the previous batch reached the sink, so a slow sink slows the source down. `Batch` is
`Rows(rows)`, `RowsAck(rows, token)` (acknowledge `token` once the rows committed; empty rows
still get their token acknowledged), `Data { rows, ack, redelivered }` (`redelivered` forces
`check_existing`), `Timeout` or `End` (the host closes the subscription and subscribes again
after a backoff). Rows are JSON objects, as `fetch` returns them. The optional module-level
`fn ack(tokens: &[u64])` (it may also take `connector: &Connector`) runs after the
subscription's own `ack`; a type implementing `Subscription` may instead override
`ack(&mut self, tokens)` and `close(&mut self)`. The returned closure lives beyond the call,
so it cannot borrow `pipe` or `kwargs`: copy what it needs, as `station` above (Meerschaum adds
`+ use<>` to an `impl` return type for you, so a borrow is reported at your line).

A producer thread can feed a `ChannelSubscription`, as in the Cargo SDK: a full channel blocks
the producer, and the subscription ends when every sender is dropped.

```rust
#[make_connector]
mod feed {
    fn subscribe(pipe: &Pipe) -> Result<Box<dyn Subscription>> {
        let count = pipe.parameters()["fetch"]["count"].as_u64().unwrap_or(3);
        let (sender, subscription) = ChannelSubscription::new(1);
        std::thread::spawn(move || {
            for id in 0..count {
                let rows = Frame::from_rows(vec![json!({"id": id})]).unwrap();
                if sender.send(rows).is_err() {
                    return;
                }
            }
        });
        Ok(Box::new(subscription))
    }
}
```

### Instance connectors

`#[make_connector(instance)]` (or `instance = true`) makes the module's connector type an
instance, the counterpart of a Python connector with `IS_INSTANCE = True`: `-i <type>:<label>`
then registers, syncs, lists and deletes pipes through it. Its functions named after the
instance methods answer them; others are helpers. A method you leave out is "not
implemented", so the host falls back where it can (file-based leases, for example). The module
may also define `fetch`, `sync` and `subscribe`, as a source connector does.

```rust
/// Pipes and rows in memory.
#[make_connector(instance)]
mod memory {
    use std::collections::BTreeMap;
    use std::sync::Mutex;
    static ROWS: Mutex<BTreeMap<String, Vec<Value>>> = Mutex::new(BTreeMap::new());

    fn key(pipe: &Pipe) -> String { format!("{}|{}", pipe.connector_keys(), pipe.metric_key()) }

    fn register_pipe(pipe: &Pipe) -> SuccessTuple {
        ROWS.lock().unwrap().entry(key(pipe)).or_default();
        SuccessTuple::success()
    }
    fn pipe_exists(pipe: &Pipe) -> bool { ROWS.lock().unwrap().contains_key(&key(pipe)) }
    fn sync_pipe(pipe: &Pipe, data: Vec<Value>) -> (bool, String) {
        let count = data.len();
        ROWS.lock().unwrap().entry(key(pipe)).or_default().extend(data);
        (true, format!("Inserted {count} rows."))
    }
    fn get_pipe_data(pipe: &Pipe, begin: Option<Bound>, params: &Value) -> Vec<Value> {
        ROWS.lock().unwrap().get(&key(pipe)).cloned().unwrap_or_default()
    }
    fn get_sync_time(pipe: &Pipe, newest: bool) -> Option<i64> { None }
    fn fetch_pipes_keys(query: &Value) -> Value {
        Value::Array(ROWS.lock().unwrap().keys().map(|k| {
            let (c, m) = k.split_once('|').unwrap();
            json!([c, m, null])
        }).collect())
    }
}
```

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| `register_pipe`, `delete_pipe`, `drop_pipe`, `edit_pipe`, `sync_pipe`, `clear_pipe`, `deduplicate_pipe`, `drop_pipe_indices`, `create_pipe_indices`, `compress_pipe`, `decompress_pipe`, `analyze_pipe`, `vacuum_pipe`, `partition_pipe` | `SuccessTuple`, `(bool, String)` or `(bool, &str)` |
| `get_pipe_data` | `Vec<Value>` rows, `Frame` or `Option<Frame>` |
| `test_connection`, `pipe_exists`, `acquire_pipe_lease`, `release_pipe_lease` | `bool` |
| `fetch_pipes_keys` | `[[connector_keys, metric_key, location_key], ...]` (or a map of pipe IDs to those lists) |
| `get_pipe_id`, `get_pipe_rowcount`, `get_pipe_size` | `Option<i64>` (or `i64`) |
| `get_sync_time` | an integer, an ISO timestamp string, or `None` |
| `get_pipe_attributes`, `get_pipe_columns_types`, `get_pipe_index_names`, `get_pipe_columns_indices` | a JSON object (`Value`, or any serializable map) |

Any of these may be wrapped in `Result`; the value methods may return any serializable type.
Parameters bind by name: `pipe: &Pipe`, `connector: &Connector`, `data: Option<Frame>` or
`data: Vec<Value>` (the rows of `sync_pipe`), `context: &Value` (the call's whole JSON context,
as `NativeConnector` sends it), and any field of the call: `query`, `options`
and `params` (`&Value`), `begin` / `end` (`Option<Bound>`), `select_columns`, `omit_columns`,
`limit`, `order`, `check_existing`, `chunksize`, `extra`, `newest`, `patch`, `no_policy`,
`full`, `chunk_minutes`, `holder` (`&str`) and `ttl_seconds`. A field is read from the context,
then from its `query`, then from its `options`; declare it as `&Value`, `&str`, or any owned
type it deserializes into (`bool`, `f64`, `Option<i64>`, `Option<Vec<String>>`, ...).

### Console pages

`#[web_page]` on a top-level function serves it as a page of the web console
(`meerschaum[dash]`), the counterpart of Python's `@web_page`. The path defaults to the
function's name and is served under `/dash/`; the options are Python's:

```rust
/// A report of the readings.
#[web_page("readings/report", login_required = false, page_group = "Readings")]
fn report(page: &PageRequest) -> String {
    let station = page.query_param("station").unwrap_or_default();
    format!("<h3>Readings for {station}</h3><p>Viewed by {}.</p>", page.username.as_deref().unwrap_or("a guest"))
}

#[web_page]
fn status() -> (u16, String) {
    (503, "<p>Not ready yet.</p>".into())
}
```

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| a path (first) | `"readings/report"` is served at `/dash/readings/report` (a leading `/dash/` is accepted); default: the function's name |
| `login_required = false` | Served without a console session (default `true`) |
| `skip_navbar = true` | Hide the console's navigation bar (default `false`) |
| `page_group = "..."` | The navigation group (default: the plugin's name) |
| `dark_theme = false` | Opt out of the console's dark component theme (default `true`) |

The function may take `page: &PageRequest` (`path`, the raw `query`, `query_param(name)`, and
`username`, `None` for a guest) and returns the page's HTML as a `String` or `&str`, `(u16, T)`
to set the status, or a `Result` of those (an `Err` is a `500` page showing its message). The HTML
follows the [page contract](/reference/migrating-to-v5/#option-b-the-page-contract-recommended-for-new-pages)
(`data-mrsm-figure` / `data-mrsm-map` elements). The path is checked when the plugin is built:
relative segments of letters, digits, `-` and `_`, no wildcards. Pages are fixed when the
server starts.

### Dependencies

The standard library and shorthand types need no declarations. To use an external
crate, add one optional Cargo block at the **top of the same file**:

```rust
//! ```cargo
//! [dependencies]
//! regex = "1"
//! ```

use regex::Regex;

#[make_action]
fn count_words(action: Vec<String>) -> (bool, String) {
    let words = Regex::new(r"\w+").unwrap();
    let count = words.find_iter(&action.join(" ")).count();
    (true, format!("{count} words"))
}
```

Run `mrsm count words hello world`. Cargo versions, feature lists, renamed dependencies,
Git dependencies, and local `path` dependencies use their normal Cargo syntax.
Local dependency paths resolve relative to the original `.rs` file, rather than the cache.
You can enable Serde features, for example `serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }`;
`serde_json` keeps the features required by the runtime.

Meerschaum generates the Cargo project and keeps its `Cargo.lock` in the build cache.
Unchanged plugins reuse the built library; editing a dependency declaration triggers a
rebuild. Dependencies are compiled into the plugin, so Cargo is needed for builds but
not to use an already-built library. First builds may download crates. Nothing is
installed into a Python virtual environment.

Only `[dependencies]` is supported in the inline block. Use a packaged Cargo plugin for
workspace settings, build dependencies, custom profiles, or publishing a lockfile.
Changes to external path dependencies are not fingerprinted: edit the `.rs` file or
remove its build cache after changing such a dependency. Relative `include_str!` and
other source paths still resolve from the cached source; use a Cargo plugin for assets.

### Single-file build cache

The filename supplies the plugin name; the version is `VERSION` (`0.0.0` when omitted).
Sources and build output stay under `<root>/cache/native_build/<name>/`; nothing is
written beside the original `.rs` file. Unchanged builds are reused, edits trigger
recompilation, and failed builds are remembered until an edit or cache deletion.
The small runtime is embedded by the running host; there is no published SDK dependency.
Shared Cargo dependencies live in `<root>/cache/native_build/.single_file_target/`; each
plugin has its own copied library and build stamp. Compiler diagnostics are saved in
`<root>/cache/native_build/<name>/mrsm-build-error.txt` and shown again for failed builds.

Rust returns the final expression of a function. In the example above, do **not** put
a semicolon after `vec![...]`: that would discard the rows and return `()` instead of
`Vec<Value>`.

Use the full crate layout above for multiple source files, relative included assets, typed
Arrow frames, or a hand-written manifest. Relative paths in a
shorthand file resolve from its generated copy in the cache.


---

# Routes and MCP

Source: https://meerschaum.io/reference/plugins/rust-plugins/routes-and-mcp/

# Routes and MCP in Rust Plugins

A Rust plugin can serve **HTTP routes** next to the core API (the native counterpart of
`@api_plugin`) and expose **MCP tools, resources and prompts** to agents (the counterpart of
`meerschaum.mcp.tool(...)`). Both are declared in the plugin's manifest, so `mrsm start api` and
`mrsm start mcp` know them without loading the library, and both run in-process: no Python API
host is started for them.

The complete, tested example is
[`crates/meerschaum-plugin/examples/native_api.rs`](https://github.com/bmeares/Meerschaum/blob/v5/crates/meerschaum-plugin/examples/native_api.rs).

## 🛣️ Routes

Declare each route in your plugin's manifest (`api_routes` in its entry) and implement
`Plugin::api_route`:

```rust
use meerschaum_plugin::api::{RouteRequest, RouteResponse, RouteSpec};
use meerschaum_plugin::prelude::*;

#[derive(Default)]
struct Items;

impl Plugin for Items {
    fn manifest(&self) -> Value {
        Manifest::new()
            .api_route(RouteSpec::new("get_item", "GET", "/items/{id}").scopes(["pipes:read"]))
            .api_route(RouteSpec::new("upload", "PUT", "/items/files/{*key}").scopes(["pipes:write"]))
            .api_route(RouteSpec::new("health", "GET", "/items-health").public())
            .into()
    }

    fn api_route(&self, request: &RouteRequest) -> Result<RouteResponse> {
        Ok(match request.name.as_str() {
            "get_item" => RouteResponse::json(&json!({
                "id": request.path_param("id"),
                "fields": request.query_params.get("field"),
                "caller": request.principal,
            })),
            "upload" => RouteResponse::empty(204).header("x-stored", request.body.len().to_string()),
            _ => RouteResponse::text("ok"),
        })
    }
}

meerschaum_plugin::export_plugin!(Items);
```

### Declaring a route

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | The route's name within the plugin; the request carries it back (`request.name`). |
| `method` | Any HTTP method (`GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS`, or an extension method such as `PROPFIND`), or `*` for every method. Default `GET`. Several routes may share a path with different methods; another method is a `405` with an `Allow` header, and `HEAD` falls back to the `GET` route (without a body). |
| `path` | A path with parameters (see [Paths](#paths)). |
| `scopes` | Scopes the caller must hold, such as `pipes:read`. A caller holding `*` holds all of them. |
| `public` | Serve without credentials. When the caller sends valid credentials anyway, the principal is still passed. A public route may not declare `scopes` (it is refused at startup). |
| `description` | Optional text for people reading the manifest. |

#### Paths

Paths follow Starlette's syntax (what `@api_plugin` routes use), one parameter per segment:

| Segment | Matches |
|---|---|
| `items` | The literal text. |
| `{id}` or `{id:str}` | Any non-empty segment. |
| `{id}.json`, `v{n}` | A parameter with a static prefix or suffix (`/docs/{name}.json` matches `/docs/a.b.json` with `name = "a.b"`). |
| `{n:int}`, `{x:float}`, `{u:uuid}` | Digits; digits with an optional fraction; a hyphenated UUID. Values still arrive as strings. |
| `{*rest}` or `{rest:path}` | The rest of the path, slashes included (last segment only, not empty). |

Values are percent-decoded. When several routes of a plugin match the same request (for example
`/docs/{name}.json` and `/docs/{n:int}`), each is tried in declaration order and the first one
that matches the path and the method serves it. A path that matches no route is a `404`.

A route needs the core API's credentials (a login token or an API key) and every scope it
declares, with the same `401` and `403 {"detail": "Missing required scope: '<scope>'"}`
answers as the core routes. Under `--no-auth`, every route is open and the caller holds `*`.

### Refused routes

When the server starts, it refuses (and skips, with one line on stderr naming the plugin, the
route and the reason) any route that:

- would **shadow a core route**: a core route group (`/pipes`, `/users`, `/actions`, `/jobs`,
  `/engine`, `/mcp`, `/login`, `/docs`, `/`, ...), the console (`/dash`) and its page routes
  (`/_pages`, which serve plugin pages and their assets), `/static`, the web terminal, or the
  server's internal `/_mrsm/` routes;
- has a parameter in its first segment (`/{x}/...`, `/x{id}`), which would capture unmatched paths;
- conflicts with a route another native plugin mounted first, or repeats a method on the same
  path (`/a/{id}` and `/a/{other}` are the same path);
- is `public` and declares `scopes`;
- belongs to a route group that `api:permissions:routes` disables;
- has invalid syntax (`:id` instead of `{id}`, two parameters in one segment, an unknown
  converter, a catch-all that is not last or not a whole segment, `..`, `%`).

```text
Native plugin 'items': route GET /pipes/items is refused: it would shadow the core route group 'pipes'.
```

The rest of the plugin's routes are still served.

### The request

`RouteRequest` is the whole HTTP request:

| Field | Contents |
|---|---|
| `name`, `route_path` | The matched route's name and declared path. |
| `method`, `path` | The request method (uppercase) and path. |
| `path_params` | `{"id": "42"}`, percent-decoded. `request.path_param("id")`. |
| `query`, `query_params` | The raw query string, and every decoded value of each key in order (`{"q": ["a", "b"]}`). `request.query_param("q")` returns the first. |
| `headers` | Lowercase names to every value. `authorization` is removed (the server already authenticated the caller), and so is the console's session cookie (`mrsm-session-id`) from `cookie`; other cookies are kept. `request.header("X-Name")` is case-insensitive and `request.cookie("theme")` reads one cookie. |
| `body` | The body as bytes (up to 64 MiB: a larger body is a `413`, one that cannot be read a `400`). `request.text()` and `request.json::<T>()` decode it. |
| `principal` | `None` when anonymous, else `{"kind": "user", "username", "user_id", "user_type"}` or `{"kind": "token", "token_id", "label", "user_id"}`. No secrets. |
| `scopes` | The caller's granted scopes (`["*"]` under `--no-auth`). `request.has_scope("x")`. |

### The response

`RouteResponse` carries a status, headers (several values of one name are kept, such as two
`set-cookie` headers) and body bytes:

```rust
RouteResponse::json(&value)                         // 200 application/json
RouteResponse::text("hello")                        // 200 text/plain; charset=utf-8
RouteResponse::bytes("image/png", png_bytes)        // any content type
RouteResponse::empty(204)
RouteResponse::error(404, "No such item.")          // {"detail": "No such item."}, like the core API
RouteResponse::text("moved").with_status(307).header("location", "/items/1")
```

An `Err` from `api_route` becomes `500 {"detail": "<message>"}`.

## ⚙️ How calls run

- **Concurrently.** Like FastAPI with `@api_plugin`, the server runs requests in parallel: each
  `api_route`, `mcp_tool`, `mcp_resource` and `mcp_prompt` call runs on its own thread and is
  not serialized with the plugin's other calls, so a slow route holds up neither the plugin's
  other routes nor its MCP entries. These methods must therefore be thread-safe; the SDK builds a
  fresh `P::default()` for every call, so a plugin with no shared state needs nothing more.
- **For the caller.** A handler's [host calls](advanced.md#talking-to-meerschaum)
  (`host::pipe(...)`, `pipe.get_data(...)`, `host::read_sql(...)`, ...) act for the request's
  caller, with the scopes the core API requires: `pipes:read` to read pipes, `pipes:write` to
  sync, `pipes:delete` to clear, `pipes:register` to register, `sql:read` for read-only `read_sql`
  queries, and for `exec_sql`
  `actions:execute` and a caller who may run actions (an administrator, unless the server lets
  other users run actions). A refused call returns an `Err` naming the reason, so a handler can
  answer `403` (`RouteResponse::error(403, error.to_string())`). SQL from a route never reaches
  Meerschaum's internal tables (`mrsm_users`, `mrsm_tokens`, ...). An anonymous caller of a
  public route has no scopes unless the route declares `host_scopes`
  (`#[api_route(GET, "/status", public = true, host_scopes = ["pipes:read"])]`,
  `RouteSpec::new(...).public().host_scopes(["pipes:read"])`): every caller's host calls get them
  on top of its own. These grants preserve pipe visibility, edit rights and connector teams;
  anonymous callers can reach Everyone's pipes. Under `--no-auth` and over MCP stdio every call
  is allowed. Pipes and named SQL stay on the instances the server allows, and a Pipe without
  instance keys is on the server's instance. SQL also refuses targets of hidden pipes.
  [Talking to Meerschaum](advanced.md#talking-to-meerschaum) has the full rules.
- **Bounded.** At most 32 server calls of one plugin run at once (routes and MCP entries are
  counted separately). Up to 16 further requests wait up to 30 seconds for a free slot; any
  beyond those, and any that wait too long, answer
  `503 {"detail": "Native plugin '<name>' is busy ..."}` with `Retry-After: 1` (an MCP call
  returns that message as its error). A route's request body is read only once it holds a slot,
  so waiting and refused requests buffer nothing. A call that never returns keeps its slot, so a
  stuck handler degrades into `503`s rather than unbounded threads and memory.
- **Fixed at startup.** Routes and MCP entries are read from the manifests when `mrsm start api`
  (or `mrsm start mcp`) starts. Installing, updating or removing a native plugin takes effect
  after a restart; unlike Python plugins, the running server does not pick it up.

## 🤖 MCP tools, resources and prompts

Declare entries under `mcp_tools`, `mcp_resources` and `mcp_prompts` and implement the matching
`Plugin` methods:

```rust
use meerschaum_plugin::mcp::{
    PromptGet, ResourceContents, ResourceRead, ToolCall, ToolSpec, message,
};

// In `manifest()`:
//   Manifest::new()
//       .mcp_tool(ToolSpec::new("count_items", "Count the items of a kind.")
//           .input_schema(json!({"type": "object",
//               "properties": {"kind": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["kind"]}))
//           .scopes(["pipes:read"])
//           .read_only())
//       .mcp_resource(serde_json::from_value(json!({"name": "item", "description": "One item.",
//           "uri_template": "items://{id}", "scopes": ["pipes:read"]}))?)
//       .mcp_prompt(serde_json::from_value(json!({"name": "summarize",
//           "description": "Summarize an item.", "arguments": [{"name": "id", "required": true}]}))?)

fn mcp_tool(&self, call: &ToolCall) -> Result<Value> {
    let kind = call.argument("kind").and_then(Value::as_str).unwrap_or_default();
    Ok(json!({"kind": kind, "count": 3}))
}

fn mcp_resource(&self, read: &ResourceRead) -> Result<ResourceContents> {
    Ok(ResourceContents::json(&json!({"id": read.variable("id")})))
}

fn mcp_prompt(&self, get: &PromptGet) -> Result<Value> {
    Ok(json!({"messages": [message("user", format!("Summarize item {}.", get.argument("id").unwrap_or("?")))]}))
}
```

| Entry | Keys | Called with | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mcp_tools` | `name`, `description`, `input_schema` (JSON Schema), `output_schema`?, `scopes`, `title`?, `annotations`? (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`, `idempotentHint`, `openWorldHint`) | `ToolCall {name, arguments, principal, scopes}` | Any JSON value. A string is sent as the text content as is; anything else as indented JSON, and also as `structuredContent` when the tool declares an `output_schema` and the value is an object. |
| `mcp_resources` | `name`, `description`, `uri` or `uri_template` (`{var}` matches one path segment), `mime_type`? (default `application/json`), `scopes`, `title`? | `ResourceRead {name, uri, variables, principal, scopes}` | `ResourceContents::text`, `::json` or `::blob` (sent base64-encoded). |
| `mcp_prompts` | `name`, `description`?, `title`?, `arguments` (`[{name, description?, required?}]`), `scopes` | `PromptGet {name, arguments, principal, scopes}` | A string (one user message), a list of messages, or `{"description"?, "messages"}`. |

Native entries follow the same rules as built-in and Python plugin entries:

- An entry whose `scopes` the caller does not hold is **hidden** from the lists and refused if
  called. Over stdio (`mrsm start mcp`) the caller holds `*`.
- A read-only server (`api:mcp:read_only`) hides tools without `readOnlyHint: true`, and prompts
  whose scopes end in `:write`, `:delete`, `:drop` or `:execute`.
- Tool arguments are **validated against `input_schema`** before your method runs; a violation
  is a tool error (`Invalid arguments for '<tool>': ...`) that the model sees. Prompt arguments
  are checked against the declared `arguments`.
- A native tool or prompt never replaces a built-in one of the same name, and a native resource
  never takes a built-in resource's URI: such an entry is hidden, with one line on stderr at
  startup (`Native plugin 'items': MCP tool 'list_pipes' is hidden: a built-in tool has that
  name.`), as is an entry whose name another native plugin declared first. A native tool or
  prompt replaces a Python plugin's tool or prompt of the same name.
- An `Err` from a tool is a tool error (`isError: true`) with your message; from a resource or a
  prompt, a JSON-RPC error.

## 🧱 Without the typed methods

Plugins that implement `Plugin::call` themselves receive these call kinds as `request.method`
with JSON contexts, and can forward them with `meerschaum_plugin::sdk::call_server_extension`:

| Method | Context | Reply |
|---|---|---|
| `api_route` | `RouteRequest` as JSON; the body is `body_base64` | `{"status"?, "headers"?: {"name": ["v", ...]}, "body_base64"?}`; the host also accepts `"json": <value>`, `"body": "<text>"` and `"content_type"` |
| `mcp_tool` | `{"name", "arguments", "principal", "scopes"}` | the result value |
| `mcp_resource` | `{"name", "uri", "variables", "principal", "scopes"}` | a string, `{"text", "mime_type"?}` or `{"blob_base64", "mime_type"?}` |
| `mcp_prompt` | `{"name", "arguments", "principal", "scopes"}` | a string, a list of messages, or `{"description"?, "messages"}` |

These travel through the same `invoke` entry point as every other method: the ABI version is
unchanged, and plugins built before these call kinds existed keep loading.

### Plugins with `routes` and `route`

The first native route adapter asked a plugin whose manifest lists a name under `api_plugins`
for `routes` (`[{"method", "path", "public"?}]`) and served each request through `route`
(`{method, path, query, body, user}` with a text body; reply `{status, content_type, body}`).
Such plugins keep working unchanged, with static paths: their replies are parsed as before (an
invalid or missing `status` is `200`, `content_type` defaults to `text/plain; charset=utf-8`),
and their `route` calls stay serialized with the plugin's other calls. They now authenticate
like the core routes, so an API key works on a non-public route as well as a login token.
Declare `api_routes` instead to get path parameters, scopes, headers, byte bodies and concurrent
calls; a plugin that declares `api_routes` is never asked for `routes`.

## 📄 Single-file plugins

A single `.rs` file declares routes and MCP entries with attributes on top-level functions;
Meerschaum writes the manifest entries and the dispatch for you:

```rust
/// One item (the doc comment is the route's description).
#[api_route(GET, "/items/{id:int}", scopes = ["pipes:read"])]
fn item(request: &RouteRequest) -> Value {
    json!({"id": request.path_param("id"), "user": request.principal})
}

/// Add two integers.
#[mcp_tool(read_only = true, input_schema = r#"{"type": "object", "properties": {"a": {"type": "integer"}, "b": {"type": "integer"}}, "required": ["a", "b"]}"#)]
fn add(arguments: &Value) -> Value {
    json!({"sum": arguments["a"].as_i64().unwrap_or(0) + arguments["b"].as_i64().unwrap_or(0)})
}

/// One item as a resource.
#[mcp_resource(uri_template = "items://{id}")]
fn item_resource(resource: &ResourceRead) -> ResourceContents {
    ResourceContents::json(&json!({"id": resource.variable("id")}))
}

#[mcp_prompt(description = "Greet someone.", arguments = ["who"])]
fn greet(prompt: &PromptGet) -> String {
    format!("Say hello to {}.", prompt.argument("who").unwrap_or("nobody"))
}
```

`#[api_route]` takes the method (`GET`, `"post"`, `"*"`; `GET` when only the path is given),
the path and `scopes`, `public`, `name` and `description`. The MCP attributes take `name`,
`description` (default: the doc comment), `title` and `scopes`, plus `input_schema`,
`output_schema`, `read_only` and `annotations` for tools, `uri` or `uri_template` and
`mime_type` for resources, and `arguments` for prompts. The request, call, read and prompt
types and the accepted return types match the SDK's; the
[single-file reference](advanced.md#api-routes) lists them. The same server rules apply:
calls run concurrently, a public route may not require scopes, a path must follow the
[path rules](#paths) and may not shadow a core route (the plugin then fails to build with the
message, at the path's line, instead of the server refusing the route at startup), and routes
and entries are fixed when the server starts. A prompt message with another role is
`meerschaum_plugin::mcp::message("assistant", text)`.

## 🧪 Testing

```bash
cargo test -p meerschaum-plugin --test api_mcp           # the call kinds through the ABI
cargo test -p meerschaum-server --test native_extensions  # mounting, auth, refusals, MCP dispatch
cargo test -p meerschaum-cli --test native_api_mcp        # `mrsm start api` and `mrsm start mcp`
```

To try your own plugin, start a server on a scratch root and call a route and a tool:

```bash
mrsm start api -i sql:local --host 127.0.0.1 -p 8224 --no-dash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:8224/items/42?field=a
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' http://127.0.0.1:8224/mcp \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"count_items","arguments":{"kind":"a"}}}'
```

# Executors and Streams

Source: https://meerschaum.io/reference/plugins/rust-plugins/executors-and-streams/

# Executors and Streaming Connectors in Rust Plugins

A Rust plugin can provide a **job executor** (the native counterpart of `@make_executor`) and
**streaming connectors** whose data `mrsm sync pipes --listen` lands as it arrives (the
counterpart of an `IS_STREAMING` connector's `subscribe`). Both run in-process; no Python worker
is started for them.

The complete, tested examples are
[`native_executor.rs`](https://github.com/bmeares/Meerschaum/blob/v5/crates/meerschaum-plugin/examples/native_executor.rs)
(a `procs:<label>` executor that runs each job as a local process) and
[`native_stream.rs`](https://github.com/bmeares/Meerschaum/blob/v5/crates/meerschaum-plugin/examples/native_stream.rs)
(a `ticker:<label>` streaming connector and a plugin-level `subscribe`).

## 👷 Executors

An executor manages [background jobs](../../background-jobs/executors.md) by name. Declare its
type under the manifest's top-level `executor_types` and return it from `Plugin::executor`:

```rust
use meerschaum_plugin::executor::{Executor, mrsm_command};
use meerschaum_plugin::prelude::*;

#[derive(Default)]
struct Procs;

impl Plugin for Procs {
    fn manifest(&self) -> Value {
        Manifest::new()
            .executor_type(
                "procs",
                ["get_job_names", "get_job_metadata", "create_job"],
                "Run jobs as local processes.",
            )
            .into()
    }

    fn executor(&self, request: &Request) -> Option<Box<dyn Executor>> {
        // `request.label` is the label of `procs:<label>`, `request.config` its configuration,
        // `request.context["root_dir"]` the Meerschaum root the jobs belong to.
        (request.connector_type == "procs").then(|| Box::new(ProcsExecutor) as _)
    }
}

struct ProcsExecutor;

impl Executor for ProcsExecutor {
    fn get_job_names(&self) -> Result<Vec<String>> { /* ... */ Ok(vec![]) }
    fn get_job_metadata(&self, name: &str) -> Result<Value> { /* ... */ Ok(Value::Null) }
    fn create_job(&self, name: &str, sysargs: &[String], properties: &Value) -> Result<SuccessTuple> {
        // Start `mrsm <sysargs>` with `mrsm_command()` (the host's own `mrsm`), then report.
        Ok(SuccessTuple::ok(format!("Started job '{name}'.")))
    }
    // start_job, stop_job, delete_job, get_logs, monitor_logs, ...
}

meerschaum_plugin::export_plugin!(Procs);
```

Then use `procs:<label>` wherever executor keys are accepted:

```bash
mrsm sync pipes -c plugin:noaa -d -e procs:main --name noaa
mrsm show jobs -e procs:main
mrsm show logs noaa -e procs:main
mrsm stop jobs noaa -e procs:main
```

The shell's `executor procs:main` command, `meerschaum:executor` in your configuration (also
in a compose project's `config`) and `mrsm.Job(..., executor_keys='procs:main')` in Python work
the same way; in Python, `job.executor` is a `NativeExecutor` with the methods of
`meerschaum.jobs.Executor`. Shell and command-line completion suggest the declared types
(`procs:main`, or the configured labels). The executor's configuration is the connector
configuration of `procs:<label>` (`meerschaum:connectors:procs:<label>` in `edit config`, or
`MRSM_PROCS_<LABEL>`). Every method may make
[host calls](advanced.md#talking-to-meerschaum) (`host::plugin_config()`, `host::pipe(...)`),
with the trust of the process that uses the executor.

The API server's `/jobs` routes (and the web console and MCP job tools) manage the server's
local jobs only, as in v4; plugin executors are reached from the command line, the shell,
configuration, compose and Python.

### The methods

`Executor` mirrors Python's `meerschaum.jobs.Executor`. Every method has a default, so you
implement only what your executor supports:

| Method | Returns | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `get_job_names()` | every job, hidden ones included | not supported |
| `get_job_exists(name)` | `bool` | `name` in `get_job_names()` |
| `get_jobs()` | `{name: metadata}` | `get_job_names()` + `get_job_metadata()` |
| `get_job_metadata(name)` | metadata, or `Value::Null` when the job does not exist | not supported |
| `get_job_properties(name)` | the job's properties | `metadata.daemon.properties` |
| `get_job_status(name)` | `running`, `paused` or `stopped` | `metadata.daemon.status` |
| `get_job_began` / `get_job_ended` / `get_job_paused(name)` | ISO timestamps | `properties.process.began` / `ended` / `paused` |
| `create_job(name, sysargs, properties)` | success tuple (create **and** start) | not supported |
| `start_job` / `stop_job` / `pause_job` / `delete_job(name)` | success tuple | not supported |
| `get_logs(name)` | the log text | not supported |
| `get_job_stop_time(name)` | ISO timestamp of a manual stop | not supported |
| `monitor_logs(name, options)` | a `LogStream` (see below) | not supported |
| `get_job_is_blocking_on_stdin(name)` | `bool` | not supported |
| `get_job_prompt_kwargs(name)` | the pending prompt's keyword arguments | not supported |
| `write_stdin(name, data)` | write one answer line to the job's stdin | not supported |

Metadata has the shape the local and `api:` executors report:

```json
{"sysargs": ["sync", "pipes"], "result": [true, "Success"], "restart": false,
 "daemon": {"status": "running", "pid": 4242,
            "properties": {"process": {"began": "2026-01-01T00:00:00+00:00", "ended": null}}}}
```

A method you leave out is reported to the user as
`` `pause_job` is not supported by the 'procs:main' executor. `` (actions fail with that message;
listings show such a job as `stopped` without timestamps). Any other error from a method (an I/O
error, a panic) is printed as a warning naming the executor and the method, so a broken executor
is never silently shown as a stopped job. The `sysargs` given to `create_job`
never contain `-d` or `-e` / `--executor-keys`.

**Starting a job.** A job runs `mrsm <sysargs>`. Use `executor::mrsm_command()` for the program:
it is the host's own command (the `mrsm` binary, or `python -P -m meerschaum` when Meerschaum runs
from the Python package), so the job uses the same installation and environment.

**State.** A new executor value is built for every call, so keep job state outside it: in files
(as the example does under `<root_dir>/procs_jobs/<label>/`), a database, or a static map keyed by
label. Key file state on `request.context["root_dir"]`, not on `MRSM_ROOT_DIR`: one process may
manage the jobs of several roots (`mrsm compose` runs in the host's root and manages the jobs of
each project's root).

**Following logs.** `monitor_logs` returns a `LogStream`; the host calls
`next_lines(timeout)` until you return `LogEvent::End(result)` (only when
`options.stop_on_exit` is set and the job stopped) or the user stops watching:

```rust
impl LogStream for Tail {
    fn next_lines(&mut self, timeout: Duration) -> Result<LogEvent> {
        // Return LogEvent::Lines(new_lines), LogEvent::Timeout after `timeout`,
        // or LogEvent::End(Some(result)).
    }
}
```

**Prompts.** While the host follows a job's log with input accepted (`show logs`, or `start job`
in the foreground), each `LogEvent::Timeout` makes it ask `get_job_is_blocking_on_stdin`; when
that is `true`, it reads the user's answer and calls `write_stdin(name, data)` (one line, ending
in `\n`). Executors without those two methods never receive input.

## 📡 Streaming connectors

A streaming connector pushes rows as they arrive instead of answering `fetch`. Mark the
connector type `"is_streaming": true` with `"subscribe"` in its `methods` (or list `subscribe`
under the plugin's `data_functions` for `plugin:<name>`) and implement `Plugin::subscribe`:

```rust
use meerschaum_plugin::subscribe::{Batch, ChannelSubscription, Subscription};

fn subscribe(&self, request: &Request) -> Result<Box<dyn Subscription>> {
    // `request.context["pipe"]` is the pipe, `request.context["kwargs"]` the sync's keyword
    // arguments (`begin`, `end`, `params`, `chunksize`, `check_existing`, plugin flags, ...),
    // the same ones a Python `subscribe(pipe, ..., **kwargs)` receives.
    let topic = request.context["pipe"]["parameters"]["fetch"]["topic"].clone();
    // A producer thread feeds a bounded channel: `send` blocks while the host is busy.
    let (sender, subscription) = ChannelSubscription::new(16);
    std::thread::spawn(move || {
        for frame in read_messages(topic) {
            if sender.send(frame).is_err() {
                return; // the host closed the subscription
            }
        }
    });
    Ok(Box::new(subscription))
}
```

Then listen:

```bash
mrsm register pipe -c ticker:office -m readings -i sql:local
mrsm sync pipes -c ticker:office -i sql:local --listen
```

The host **pulls**: it calls `next_batch(timeout)` on your subscription, hands each batch to the
engine's micro-batching sink (`parameters['stream']`: `idle_ms`, `max_latency_ms`, `max_rows`,
`max_bytes`) and asks again only once the sink accepted it, so a slow instance slows your source
down instead of filling memory. `next_batch` may block (on a channel, a socket, a sleep) up to the
timeout:

| Return | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Batch::data(frame)` | rows to sync |
| `Batch::with_ack(frame, token)` | rows whose `token` your `ack(tokens)` receives once they committed (acknowledge-after-commit, like MQTT QoS 1 or Kafka offsets). An empty frame with a token (a filtered message) is acknowledged with the next committed flush |
| `Batch::Timeout` | nothing new yet |
| `Batch::End` | the source ended; the engine subscribes again after a backoff |

An error from `next_batch` (or `subscribe`) closes the subscription and the engine resubscribes
with exponential backoff, emitting `stream_restarted`. Tokens belong to the subscription that
returned them: `ack` only ever receives tokens of its own subscription. Batches still buffered when
a subscription ended are never acknowledged on the next one (their source redelivers them), so a
token may be reused across subscriptions (MQTT packet ids, per-session offsets). `close()` is called once when the listener
stops. Committed flushes trigger the stream's children (`--listen --children`) exactly like a
Python `subscribe` stream. A subscription may implement `Subscription` directly instead of using
`ChannelSubscription`; the example's `ticker` does, with no thread at all.

`next_batch`, `ack` and `close` are not serialized with your plugin's other calls (one blocking
`next_batch` never holds up a `fetch` or another subscription), so share state between them only
through synchronized types. `subscribe` and each of these calls may make
[host calls](advanced.md#talking-to-meerschaum) (`pipe.get_sync_time()`, `host::plugin_config()`,
...) on their own thread, so a source can resume from the pipe's newest row or keep a cursor in
its config; a producer thread of a `ChannelSubscription` cannot.

## 🔌 The wire contract

Executors and subscriptions are ordinary JSON methods of the plugin ABI; data crosses as an Arrow
C stream like `fetch`. The SDK implements them for you; a plugin written against the C ABI
directly answers:

| Method | Context | Reply |
|---|---|---|
| `executor.<method>` (every method above) | `{name?, sysargs?, properties?, mrsm, root_dir?}` | the method's JSON value; status 3 when unsupported |
| `executor.write_stdin` | `{name, data, mrsm, root_dir?}` | `null` |
| `executor.monitor_logs` | `{name, strip_timestamps, stop_on_exit, mrsm, root_dir?}` | `{"handle": u64}` |
| `executor.next_logs` | `{handle, timeout_ms}` | `{"status": "lines" \| "timeout" \| "end", "lines": [...], "result": [bool, str] \| null}` |
| `executor.close_logs` | `{handle}` | `null` |
| `subscribe` | `{pipe, kwargs}` | `{"handle": u64}` |
| `next_batch` | `{handle, timeout_ms}` | `{"status": "batch" \| "timeout" \| "end", "ack": u64 \| null, "redelivered": bool}`, rows in the output stream |
| `ack_batches` | `{handle, tokens}` | `null` |
| `close_subscription` | `{handle}` | `null` |

For `executor.*` calls, the request's `connector_type` and `label` are the executor keys and
`config` is the executor's configuration. `mrsm` is the host's command (see above) and `root_dir`
the root the jobs belong to. For `subscribe`, `kwargs` are the sync's keyword arguments. A
`next_batch` reply with status `batch`, an `ack` and no rows is an empty batch whose token is
still acknowledged.

## 📄 Single-file plugins

A single `.rs` file declares both without a Cargo project. An executor is a module marked
`#[make_executor]`, named after the executor type (`#[make_executor(name = "...")]` to choose
another). Its functions are the methods of the table above with the same names; a method you
leave out answers "not supported", and the derived ones (`get_job_exists`, `get_jobs`,
`get_job_properties`, `get_job_status`, `get_job_began` / `_ended` / `_paused`) fall back on the
others as in the SDK:

```rust
#[make_executor]
mod procs {
    // Any function may take `executor: &ExecutorInfo`: `executor.label`, `executor.config`,
    // `executor.root_dir` (the root the jobs belong to) and `executor.mrsm` (the command that
    // starts `mrsm <sysargs>`).
    fn get_job_names(executor: &ExecutorInfo) -> Vec<String> { /* ... */ }
    fn get_job_metadata(executor: &ExecutorInfo, name: &str) -> Value { /* null when missing */ }
    fn create_job(executor: &ExecutorInfo, name: &str, sysargs: Vec<String>, properties: &Value) -> (bool, String) { /* ... */ }
    fn stop_job(name: &str) -> (bool, String) { /* ... */ }
    fn get_logs(executor: &ExecutorInfo, name: &str) -> Option<String> { /* ... */ }
    fn write_stdin(name: &str, data: &str) -> Result<()> { /* ... */ }
    // Each call is one `next_logs`. `show logs` follows a job through this method; without
    // it, only `show logs --nopretty` (which reads `get_logs`) shows the logs.
    fn monitor_logs(name: &str, stop_on_exit: bool) -> impl FnMut(Duration) -> LogEvent { /* ... */ }
}
```

Every function may also return a `Result` of its type, and `SuccessTuple` is accepted wherever
`(bool, String)` is.

A streaming connector is a `fn subscribe` inside a `#[make_connector]` module (or at the top
level, for `plugin:<name>`). It receives the pipe, the connector and the sync's keyword arguments
and returns a closure the host calls for each `next_batch`, a value of a type implementing
`Subscription`, or the SDK's `Box<dyn Subscription>` (a `ChannelSubscription` fed by a producer
thread works too). A `subscribe` with other parameters or another return type is an ordinary
helper:

```rust
#[make_connector]
mod ticker {
    fn subscribe(pipe: &Pipe, kwargs: &Value) -> Result<impl FnMut(Duration) -> Batch> {
        let mut next = 0;
        Ok(move |_timeout: Duration| {
            next += 1;
            // Batch::Rows(rows), Batch::RowsAck(rows, token), Batch::Data { rows, ack,
            // redelivered }, Batch::Timeout or Batch::End.
            Batch::RowsAck(vec![json!({"id": next})], next)
        })
    }
    // Optional: called with the committed tokens.
    fn ack(tokens: &[u64]) -> Result<()> { Ok(()) }
}
```

Rows are JSON objects (`Vec<Value>`) as `fetch` returns them; the rows ABI carries them in the
`next_batch` reply's `data`, with the same `status`, `ack` and `redelivered` fields as the table
above. The closure may block up to its timeout. Dropping it closes the subscription. The
[single-file reference](advanced.md#executors) lists every parameter and return type.


---

# 🚀 Repositories

Source: https://meerschaum.io/reference/plugins/repositories/

# 🚀 Repositories

Meerschaum gives you the ability to easily install and create plugins. Refer to the guide below on how to install, write, and publish plugins.

## Installing Plugins

To install plugins, run the `install plugins` command, followed by the names of the plugins you wish to install, for example:
```bash
install plugins noaa color
```

If you would like to install plugins from a private Meerschaum repository, you can specify from where you would like to download the plugin with the  `--repository` or  `-r` flag.  For example, to install the plugin   `example` from your private Meerschaum API `api:myapi`, you would execute:

```bash
install plugins example -r api:myapi
```

!!! info
    [Any Meerschaum API instance can act as a Meerschaum repository](/reference/connectors/#instances-and-repositories), and the default repository is the public `api.mrsm.io` repository. Follow the steps below to change your default repository to a private repository:

    1. Open your configuration file with `edit config`.
        ```
        mrsm edit config
        ```
    2. Change value of `meerschaum:default_repository` to the [Connector Keys](/reference/connectors) of your repository.
        ```yaml
        default_repository: api:myrepo
        ```

### Hosting Plugins
If you've [written](/reference/plugins/writing-plugins/) or installed plugins, you can host them on your own private repository. You will need a user login to your private repostitory to host plugins. Replace the values in angle brackets (`<>`) with your own values.

1. Create a user account on your [Meerschaum instance](/reference/connectors/#instances-and-repositories) with `register user <username>`.
  *If you are connecting to an existing repository, skip to step 3.*

2. Start the API server with `start api`.

3. Register and upload the plugin to your private repository with `register plugin <plugin> --repo api:<label>`.
  *If you're uploading to your own machine, use `api:local` as the repository.*

## Using Plugins
How you use a plugin depends on its [type](/reference/plugins/types-of-plugins/): whether it's a [data](/reference/plugins/types-of-plugins/#data-plugins), [action](/reference/plugins/types-of-plugins/#action-plugins), or [API](/reference/plugins/types-of-plugins/#api-plugins) plugin, and sometimes plugins can be all three.

To use a data plugin (e.g. `noaa`), bootstrap a pipe and choose the the plugin as the [connector](/reference/connectors/#connectors) (e.g. `plugin:noaa`).

To use an action plugin, simply execute the new actions provided by the plugin. You can see the available actions with `show actions`.

To use an API plugin, launch the web API with `start api`.
