# 🌳 Environment Variables

Source: https://meerschaum.io/reference/environment/

# 🌳 Environment Variables

You can manage the behavior of Meerschaum and emulate multiple installations with environment variables.

The command `mrsm show environment` will print out your current set `MRSM_` variables. For example, running this command in the Web Console reveals how the configuration is managed to subprocesses by the web server.

<img src="/assets/screenshots/web-console-environment.png" alt="Meerschaum web console environment variables.">

## Summary

Nearly all Meerschaum environment variables begin with the prefix `MRSM_`. The most commonly used variables are summarized below; each is described in detail later on this page.

| Variable | Purpose | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `MRSM_ROOT_DIR` | Root directory holding all config, plugins, venvs, jobs, and cache. | `~/.config/meerschaum` (Windows: `%APPDATA%\Meerschaum`) |
| `MRSM_CONFIG_DIR` | Directory for configuration files (isolate secrets from the root). | `$MRSM_ROOT_DIR/config` |
| `MRSM_PLUGINS_DIR` | Directory (or colon-separated list / JSON list) for plugins. | `$MRSM_ROOT_DIR/plugins` |
| `MRSM_VENVS_DIR` | Directory for virtual environments. | `$MRSM_ROOT_DIR/venvs` |
| `MRSM_WORK_DIR` | Base directory under which the root directory is created when `MRSM_ROOT_DIR` is unset. | current working directory |
| `MRSM_CONFIG` | Inline JSON or simplified-dictionary patch applied to the configuration. | _(unset)_ |
| `MRSM_PATCH` | A second patch applied *after* `MRSM_CONFIG` (may reference its keys). | _(unset)_ |
| `MRSM_<TYPE>_<LABEL>` | Define a connector by URI (e.g. `MRSM_SQL_MAIN`, `MRSM_API_MAIN`). Only variables of an existing connector type are read. | _(unset)_ |
| `MRSM_CONNECT_TIMEOUT` | Seconds to wait for the first connection of a SQL, API or Valkey connector; overrides every connector's `connect_timeout` attribute. | `5` |
| `MRSM_RUNTIME` | Marks a special runtime (e.g. `docker`). | _(unset)_ |
| `MRSM_NO_AUTO_INSTALL` | Disable every implicit package installation (imports, dependency checks, `uv`/`pip` bootstraps). | _(unset)_ |
| `MRSM_NOASK` / `MRSM_NONINTERACTIVE` | Disable interactive prompts (assume defaults). | _(unset)_ |
| `MRSM_ALLOW_PROTECTED` | `1` allows writes to connectors marked `protected: true` for this process and its children (like `--allow-protected`). | _(unset)_ |
| `MRSM_DATAFRAME` | `polars` or `pandas`: the DataFrame library Python APIs return, for this process and the jobs and workers it starts (overrides `meerschaum:dataframe`). | _(unset: `dataframe` in `meerschaum.yaml`)_ |
| `MRSM_DUCKDB_LIB` | Path to DuckDB's shared library; explicitly selects the native C API and prevents mixed Python SQLAlchemy access. | _(unset: Python driver when installed; otherwise native library lookup)_ |
| `MRSM_BIN` | Run a standalone `mrsm` binary instead of the in-process CLI of the Python package. | _(unset)_ |
| `MRSM_PYTHON` | The Python interpreter the binary runs plugin workers and `upgrade meerschaum` with. | _(auto-detected)_ |
| `MRSM_WORKER_STARTUP_TIMEOUT` | Seconds a Python worker may take to connect and say hello before it is killed and refused (for 10 s only). | `60` |
| `NO_COLOR` | Any non-empty value prints plain text, without colors or other styles (see [Colors and Plain Output](/reference/actions/#colors-and-plain-output)). | _(unset)_ |
| `FORCE_COLOR` | Style the output even when it does not go to a terminal (any value but `0`, `false` or `no`). | _(unset: styles only on a terminal and in jobs)_ |

!!! tip "Inspecting your environment"
    Run `mrsm show environment` to list every currently set `MRSM_` variable. Run `mrsm show config` to inspect the resolved configuration after all patches and connectors have been applied.

## **`MRSM_ROOT_DIR`**

By default, your root Meerschaum directory is located in `~/.config/meerschaum` (Windows: `%APPDATA%\Meerschaum`). This is similar to how your base `pip` environment behaves: with `pip`, you isolate packages in virtual environments, and with Meerschaum, you can create an isolated environment by specifying an alternative root directory. This will recreate your configuration files and virtual environments as if you were running a clean installation.

```bash
mkdir foo
MRSM_ROOT_DIR=foo \
  mrsm show environment
```

## **`MRSM_CONFIG_DIR`**

Not to be confused with `MRSM_CONFIG`, setting `MRSM_CONFIG_DIR` allows you to designate a separate directory outside of the root to isolate your secrets and segment your configuration. If unset, the default directory is `$MRSM_ROOT_DIR/config`.

## **`MRSM_PLUGINS_DIR`**

Like `MRSM_ROOT_DIR`, `MRSM_PLUGINS_DIR` lets you isolate your plugins, e.g. if you wanted to manage your plugins in a version control system like `git`.

```bash
mkdir plugins
touch plugins/example.py

MRSM_PLUGINS_DIR=plugins \
  mrsm show plugins
```

### Multiple Plugins Directories

To allow you to group plugins together, Meerschaum supports loading multiple plugins directories at once. Simply separate the paths with a colon like you would for `$PATH`:

```bash
export MRSM_PLUGINS_DIR='./plugins:/another/plugins/path'
```

You could also set `MRSM_PLUGINS_DIR` to a JSON-encoded list of paths:

```bash
export MRSM_PLUGINS_DIR='[
    "./plugins",
    "/another/plugins/path"
]'
```

## **`MRSM_VENVS_DIR`**

Like `MRSM_PLUGINS_DIR`, you can designate a separate directory outside of the Meerschaum root to contain virtual environments. This is useful for sharing virtual environments between deployments as well as separating package data from user data (e.g. Kubernetes deployments).

```bash
MRSM_VENVS_DIR='venvs/' mrsm show plugins
```

## **`MRSM_WORK_DIR`**

`MRSM_WORK_DIR` designates the base working directory under which the root directory is located when `MRSM_ROOT_DIR` is not explicitly set. This is primarily useful for containerized deployments where the process is launched from a known location.

## **`MRSM_<TYPE>_<LABEL>`**

You can temporarily register new connectors in a variable in the form `MRSM_<TYPE>_<LABEL>`, where `<TYPE>` is the connector type, and `<LABEL>` is the label for the connector (converted to lower case). Check here for more information about [environment connectors](/reference/connectors/#environment-connectors), but in a nutshell, set the variable to the [URI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_Resource_Identifier) of your connector.

```bash
MRSM_SQL_FOO=sqlite:////tmp/temp.db \
MRSM_API_BAR=http://user:pass@localhost:8000 \
  mrsm show connectors
```

Common examples are the default connectors `sql:main` and `api:main`:

```bash
MRSM_SQL_MAIN=postgresql://user:pass@localhost:5432/db \
MRSM_API_MAIN=https://user:pass@api.example.com \
  mrsm show connectors
```

You may also set the variable to a JSON object of connector attributes instead of a URI:

```bash
MRSM_SQL_FOO='{"flavor": "sqlite", "database": "/tmp/temp.db"}' \
  mrsm show connectors
```

!!! note "Reserved names"
    Names that match the reserved Meerschaum variables (e.g. `MRSM_ROOT_DIR`, `MRSM_CONFIG`) are *not* interpreted as connectors.

!!! note "Only real connector types"
    Only a variable whose `<TYPE>` is a connector type that exists becomes a connector: the built-in types (`sql`, `api`, `valkey`, `plugin`, `systemd`) and the types your plugins register with `@make_connector`. Any other `MRSM_<X>_<Y>` variable (`MRSM_DUCKDB_LIB`, `MRSM_TEST_PG_URI`, a variable a plugin reads itself) is ignored instead of turning into a connector such as `duckdb:lib` (as it did in v4).

## **`MRSM_CONNECT_TIMEOUT`**

A SQL, API or Valkey connector fails fast when its server cannot be reached. The first connection a command makes reports a refused connection, an unknown host or rejected credentials at once (`sql:main: cannot connect to localhost:5432 (connection refused). Is the database running?`), and gives up on a host that does not answer after `connect_timeout` seconds (5 by default). Set the `connect_timeout` attribute on a connector to change it for that connector, or `MRSM_CONNECT_TIMEOUT` to change it for all of them:

```bash
MRSM_CONNECT_TIMEOUT=2 mrsm show pipes -i sql:main
```

A long-running job that loses a connection it had already established keeps retrying as before.

## **`MRSM_CONFIG`**

You may patch your existing configuration with `MRSM_CONFIG`. Simply set the variable to JSON or a simplified dictionary. Remember you may symlink to other keys in your configuration (see [`MRSM{}` config symlinks](#mrsm-config-symlinks) below).

```bash
MRSM_CONFIG='{"foo": {"bar": 123}}' \
  mrsm show config foo

MRSM_CONFIG='foo:123' \
  mrsm show config foo

MRSM_CONFIG='foo:MRSM{meerschaum:connectors:sql:main:password}' \
  mrsm show config foo
```

## **`MRSM_PATCH`**

The variable `MRSM_PATCH` behaves the same way as `MRSM_CONFIG`. The difference is that `MRSM_PATCH` is applied to your configuration *after* `MRSM_CONFIG`, so you may symlink to keys defined in `MRSM_CONFIG`.

```bash
MRSM_CONFIG='{"foo": {"bar": 123}}' \
MRSM_PATCH='baz:MRSM{foo:bar}' \
  mrsm show config baz
```

## **`MRSM_RUNTIME`**

`MRSM_RUNTIME` marks a special runtime context. For example, `MRSM_RUNTIME=docker` is set inside the official Docker image. You typically do not need to set this yourself.

## **`MRSM_NOASK` / `MRSM_NONINTERACTIVE`**

Set either of these to disable interactive prompts. When set, Meerschaum assumes default answers (equivalent to passing `--noask` / `--yes`), which is useful for automation and CI pipelines.

```bash
MRSM_NOASK=1 mrsm bootstrap pipes
```

## **`MRSM_ALLOW_PROTECTED`**

Connectors marked `protected: true` refuse every change (see
[Protected Connectors](/reference/connectors/#protected-connectors)). Set
`MRSM_ALLOW_PROTECTED=1` to allow writes for a process and the processes it starts, for example
a server whose instance is protected:

```bash
MRSM_ALLOW_PROTECTED=1 mrsm start api
```

For one command, `--allow-protected` does the same. `-y` / `--yes` never does.

## **`MRSM_DATAFRAME`**

Every Python API that returns a DataFrame (`pipe.get_data()`, `conn.read()`, `pipe.fetch()`,
`Plan.to_dataframe()`, the frames handed to plugin code) returns the library of `dataframe` in
`meerschaum.yaml`: `polars` for a new root, `pandas` for a root created before 5.0.0rc15 (see
[DataFrame library](/reference/pipes/reading/#dataframe-library)). `MRSM_DATAFRAME` overrides it
for a process, the jobs it starts and the Python workers it runs plugins in:

```bash
MRSM_DATAFRAME=pandas python my_report.py
```

`as_polars=True` / `as_pandas=True` on a call override both. Any other value is an error that names
the variable.

## **`MRSM_NO_AUTO_INSTALL`**

Meerschaum normally installs a missing optional dependency when a feature first imports it. Set
`MRSM_NO_AUTO_INSTALL=1` for locked-down, offline, or reproducible environments. Missing packages
will be reported instead of downloaded; otherwise Meerschaum warns before the first automatic download
in each process. Install the dependency group before starting Meerschaum.

The variable covers every implicit installation: `attempt_import()`, the dependency version checks
(which never install a version parser), creating a virtual environment (no `uv venv --seed`), the
API host, and the DuckDB library download (see [`MRSM_DUCKDB_LIB`](#mrsm_duckdb_lib)), including
DuckDB's own extension auto-install. Installs you ask for, such as `mrsm install packages` or `pip_install()` from your
own code, still run, but never bootstrap `uv`, `pip` or `wheel` for themselves.

```bash
MRSM_NO_AUTO_INSTALL=1 mrsm show pipes
```

## **`MRSM_DUCKDB_LIB`**

Python hosts with `meerschaum[sql-duckdb]` installed and this variable unset share the public Python
DuckDB driver between Rust Pipe operations and SQLAlchemy. An explicit `MRSM_DUCKDB_LIB` selects
the native C API instead. SQLAlchemy access is refused in that process to prevent separate database
instances from losing writes. Unset the variable and restart the interpreter to use both interfaces.
Restart after installing the extra if the process already selected the native driver.

The standalone binary and Python hosts using the native C API load DuckDB's own shared library
(`libduckdb.so`, `libduckdb.dylib` or `duckdb.dll`, version 1.4 or newer) at run time.
Meerschaum looks for it in this order:

1. `MRSM_DUCKDB_LIB`, a path to the file (for air-gapped hosts; a library that fails to load is an error);
2. the cache under `<root>/drivers/`;
3. the system library path;
4. a checksum-verified download of the official release, unless `MRSM_NO_AUTO_INSTALL` is set.

```bash
MRSM_DUCKDB_LIB=/opt/duckdb/libduckdb.so mrsm show drivers
```

Run `mrsm show drivers` to see where the library comes from, and `mrsm install driver duckdb` /
`mrsm uninstall driver duckdb` to manage the cached copy.

The native C API path refuses per-connection DuckDB options that it cannot honor, including
`access_mode=READ_ONLY`. Use the Python `sql-duckdb` extra for connections with these settings.

## **`MRSM_BIN`**

By default the `mrsm` and `meerschaum` console scripts of the Python package run the CLI inside the
installed extension. Set `MRSM_BIN` to the path of a standalone `mrsm` binary (for example one built by
`cargo install meerschaum`) to run that program instead. The binary must report the same `--version`
as the installed package. Everything Meerschaum re-launches itself for (jobs, compose, pipeline steps)
uses the same program.

## **`MRSM_PYTHON`**

The standalone `mrsm` binary runs Python plugins in a worker process. `MRSM_PYTHON` names the Python
interpreter for those workers, for package installs, and for `mrsm upgrade meerschaum` (which otherwise
refuses to guess which environment to upgrade). Inside the Python package the interpreter that is already
running is used and you do not need to set it.

Before the first worker starts, the binary checks the interpreter once (`python -P -c ...`, 10 s limit):
it must import a `meerschaum` of the same major version. A missing, stale (v4) or mismatched package, an
interpreter that cannot start, and a worker that never connects each fail at once with one message that
names the interpreter, what it found and the fix (`pip install meerschaum==<version>` or `MRSM_PYTHON`);
the refusal is remembered for a few seconds, so many pipes do not each wait. A worker has
`MRSM_WORKER_STARTUP_TIMEOUT` seconds (default 60, for connecting and the hello together) before it is
killed; raise it for a legitimately slow cold start.

## Internal Variables

The following variables are set automatically by Meerschaum (e.g. for background jobs, the `systemd` executor, and the API server) and are documented here for completeness. You generally should not set them by hand.

| Variable | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `MRSM_SERVER_ID` | Identifier of the API server instance. |
| `MRSM_DAEMON_ID` | Identifier of the running daemon (background job). |
| `MRSM_JOB` | Marks that the current process is running as a job. |
| `MRSM_BIN_EXEC` | Set by the Python launcher to the path of `MRSM_BIN` when it hands over to it; guards against a launcher re-executing itself forever. |
| `MRSM_API_HOST` | Marks the process as the Python API host (plugin routes and Dash apps). |
| `MRSM_CORE_TRACE` | Set to `1` to print per-stage timings of the native boundary to stderr (diagnostics). |
| `MRSM_SYSTEMD_LOG_PATH` | Log path used by the `systemd` job executor. |
| `MRSM_SYSTEMD_STDIN_PATH` | Stdin FIFO path used by the `systemd` job executor. |
| `MRSM_SYSTEMD_RESULT_PATH` | Result path used by the `systemd` job executor. |
| `MRSM_SYSTEMD_DELETE_JOB` | Signals the `systemd` executor to delete the job on exit. |
| `MRSM_TEST_FLAVORS` | Comma-separated DB flavors used by the test suite. |

---

## `MRSM{}` Config Symlinks

Anywhere a configuration value (or pipe parameter) is read, you may reference another key in your configuration with the `MRSM{key1:key2:key3}` syntax. The reference is resolved to the target config value **at access time**, so a single source of truth (for example, a database password) can be reused across many keys.

The path inside the braces is a colon-separated sequence of config keys, equivalent to the arguments you would pass to `get_config()`. For example, `MRSM{meerschaum:connectors:sql:main:password}` resolves to `config.meerschaum.connectors.sql.main.password`.

Symlinks are resolved by `search_and_substitute_config()` in `meerschaum/config/_read_config.py` (exported from `meerschaum.config`).

### In configuration

```bash
# Reuse the SQL main password as a top-level config value.
MRSM_CONFIG='foo:MRSM{meerschaum:connectors:sql:main:password}' \
  mrsm show config foo
```

### In a connector

```yaml
# config/connectors.yaml
sql:
  reporting:
    flavor: postgresql
    host: localhost
    database: reporting
    username: MRSM{meerschaum:connectors:sql:main:username}
    password: MRSM{meerschaum:connectors:sql:main:password}
```

Now `sql:reporting` shares credentials with `sql:main`, change them in one place.

### In a pipe parameter

```python
import meerschaum as mrsm

pipe = mrsm.Pipe('demo', 'cfg', parameters={
    'username': 'MRSM{meerschaum:connectors:sql:main:username}',
})
print(pipe.parameters['username'])  # resolved to the configured username at access time
```

!!! warning "`MRSM{}` is not `{{ Pipe() }}`"
    These are two distinct features:

    - **`MRSM{key1:key2:key3}`** references a value in your **configuration**.
    - **`{{ Pipe('ck', 'mk', 'lk') }}`** references another **pipe** (its target, columns, attributes, etc.) and is resolved when `Pipe.parameters` is accessed.

    See [Pipe Parameters → `{{ Pipe(...) }}` syntax](/reference/pipes/parameters/) for the pipe-reference feature.


---

# 🩺 Troubleshooting

Source: https://meerschaum.io/reference/troubleshooting/

# Troubleshooting

A symptom-driven guide to the most common Meerschaum issues. Each entry follows **Symptom → Cause → Fix**.

!!! tip "First step: re-run with `--debug`"
    Almost every issue is faster to diagnose with the `--debug` flag. It prints the actual SQL, the resolved sync window, and the dtypes being applied. See [Debugging tips](#debugging-tips) at the bottom of this page.

For terminology used below, see the [glossary](glossary.md). For everything else, visit [docs.meerschaum.io](https://docs.meerschaum.io).

---

## Start here: `mrsm doctor`

!!! tip "Run `mrsm doctor` first"
    One command checks the installation and tells you what is wrong and how to fix it. It is **read-only** and takes about a second: it never installs, creates, migrates or writes anything, not even on a new root (no default config files, no plugin manifest, no entry-point cache), and it never imports plugin code. It reads the plugin manifest the last command cached and warns when it is stale or missing (`mrsm reload` rebuilds it). The one caveat: opening an existing SQLite database may create its `-wal` and `-shm` files beside it. Paste its `--nopretty` output into a bug report.

```bash
mrsm doctor                  # a table: group, check, PASS / WARN / FAIL / SKIP, and the fix for each problem
mrsm doctor -i sql:main      # check another instance
mrsm doctor --nopretty       # one JSON document, for a bug report or a script
mrsm doctor --debug          # the time each check took
```

In the SDK, importing `meerschaum.actions` initializes the action registry and discovers plugins before any action runs. A subsequent `actions['doctor'](...)` call is read-only from that point; `mrsm.entry(['doctor', ...])` also avoids that initial registry import.

Every check is **PASS**, **WARN** (works, but look at it), **FAIL** (something is broken) or **SKIP** (not applicable here, the detail says why); each WARN or FAIL carries the exact command or setting that fixes it. The command fails (and exits `1`) only when a check FAILs. `--nopretty` exits `1` on a FAIL too (v4 always exited `0` with `--nopretty`), and a script can also read `summary.ok` (and `summary.fail`) of the JSON document. A sample on a machine with a Python plugin installed, where an old `meerschaum` 4.x in the user site shadows the one `mrsm` was built with:

```text
┏━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ Group      ┃ Check              ┃ Status ┃ Detail                                                ┃
┡━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│ install    │ meerschaum         │ PASS   │ 5.0.0; Python extension, in-process                   │
│            │ worker python      │ PASS   │ Python 3.13.1 at /usr/bin/python3                     │
│            │ meerschaum package │ FAIL   │ /usr/bin/python3 imports `meerschaum` 4.1.4 from      │
│            │                    │        │ /home/user/.local/lib/python3.13/site-packages/       │
│            │                    │        │ meerschaum (the user site), but this program is       │
│            │                    │        │ 5.0.0                                                 │
│            │                    │        │ Fix: remove or upgrade the stale copy                 │
│            │                    │        │ (`/usr/bin/python3 -m pip install --upgrade           │
│            │                    │        │ meerschaum`, or delete that directory), or set        │
│            │                    │        │ MRSM_PYTHON to the interpreter that has 5.0.0         │
│ paths      │ root               │ PASS   │ /home/user/.config/meerschaum (writable)              │
│            │ disk: root         │ PASS   │ /home/user/.config/meerschaum: 11.3 GB free of        │
│            │                    │        │ 214.9 GB, inodes 90% free                             │
│            │ disk: temp         │ WARN   │ /tmp: 2.1 GB free of 8.0 GB, inodes 3% free           │
│            │                    │        │ Fix: free space on the filesystem of /tmp (or point   │
│            │                    │        │ it elsewhere: MRSM_ROOT_DIR, TMPDIR)                  │
│ config     │ files              │ PASS   │ 4 config files parsed                                 │
│ instance   │ connection         │ PASS   │ sql:main (timescaledb) at localhost:5432/meerschaum   │
│            │ server version     │ PASS   │ PostgreSQL 18.1                                       │
│            │ tables             │ PASS   │ mrsm_pipes, mrsm_users, mrsm_plugins exist            │
│ extras     │ api                │ PASS   │ fastapi 0.141.1, uvicorn 0.38.0, jwt 2.13.0           │
│ ...        │                    │        │                                                       │
└────────────┴────────────────────┴────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

 💢 1 check failed (install: meerschaum package); 20 passed, 1 warning, 1 failed, 7 skipped.
```

What each group looks at:

| Group | Checks |
|---|---|
| `install` | The version and how this process runs (Python extension in-process, or a standalone binary), the build, the platform, the worker interpreter (`MRSM_PYTHON`, else `python3`) and its version, and the `meerschaum` package that interpreter imports: the same rule the worker and API host apply before importing it: a copy of another **major** version (a stale v4 in `~/.local`), a copy that looks like v4, or one speaking another worker protocol is a FAIL that names the path when Python plugins are installed (they run in that interpreter) and a WARN otherwise; another release of the same major version is a WARN naming both versions (the worker starts and warns once); extra copies on `sys.path` are a WARN. Plugins, Python connectors and the API host run in that interpreter. |
| `paths` | The root, config and plugins directories exist and are writable; free space and free inodes of the root's filesystem and of the temporary directory (WARN under 1 GB or 5% inodes, FAIL under 64 MB or 1% inodes: a full `/tmp` breaks workers). |
| `config` | The config files parse, no unknown top-level keys or removed v4 keys (`system:experimental:join_fetch: true`), the `MRSM_<TYPE>_<LABEL>` connector variables found (names only, never values; other `MRSM_*` variables are listed apart), the default instance. |
| `instance` | A connection to the default instance (or `-i`) with a 5 second limit, the server version and the Meerschaum tables (`mrsm_pipes`, `mrsm_users`, `mrsm_plugins`) for `sql:` instances; `/healthcheck` and `/version` of an `api:` instance (WARN if its version differs from the client's). A SQLite database that does not exist yet is reported, not created. With the public Python DuckDB transport, the live query is SKIPped to keep diagnostics read-only: no database or shared anchor is opened. Instances are read from the config, so a connector registered only through Python (`mrsm.get_connector(...)` with no config entry) is not known to `doctor`. |
| `drivers` | In a Python host using the public DuckDB transport, installed driver metadata and the existing policy are checked without importing DuckDB or selecting a policy. A metadata PASS does not verify importability or connectivity; missing version metadata is a WARN. Standalone/native DuckDB and Oracle use the shared-library checks (`mrsm show drivers`): a missing library is a WARN when a configured connector needs it, a FAIL for the default instance when nothing will fetch it (Oracle always; native DuckDB with `MRSM_NO_AUTO_INSTALL` or a load error), and a WARN for native DuckDB downloaded on first use. A missing native library is never installed by the doctor. |
| `extras` | Which extras (`pandas`, `polars`, `geo`, `sql`, `api`, `dash`, `shell`) the worker interpreter can import, and a WARN when an installed plugin needs one that is missing (API-host plugins need `api`, Dash plugins `dash`). An extra that is partly installed and that no plugin needs is a PASS naming the packages that are not installed. |
| `plugins` | Whether the cached plugin manifest is current (a missing or stale one is a WARN: `mrsm reload`), how many plugins are installed, the ones whose import failed, and virtual environments built by another Python than the worker's (or whose interpreter is gone). Plugin code is never imported by the doctor. |
| `jobs` | Jobs that are running, paused or stopped, jobs whose last run failed, and stale PID files. |
| `stack` | If the Docker stack's compose file exists and Docker answers, the state and health of each service (a service stopped on purpose is a WARN, a crashed or unhealthy one a FAIL). The stack is never touched. |
| `extensions` | The PostgreSQL extensions of the instance against what the server ships (see [Upgrading the stack](/reference/stack/upgrades/)). |

---

## Syncing

### Sync succeeds but no rows land

**Symptom:** `sync pipes` reports success (often `Inserted 0 rows, updated 0 rows`) but the target table stays empty or unchanged.

**Cause:** This is almost always one of:

1. **Deduplication.** `pipe.filter_existing(df)` diffs incoming rows against the overlapping window already stored. Identical rows are dropped, nothing new to insert.
2. **The sync window excluded your data.** With `begin=''` (the default), the lower bound is the pipe's *sync time* minus `fetch:backtrack_minutes`. Rows older than that window are never fetched.
3. **Backtrack too small for late-arriving / corrected data.** If a source updates rows slightly behind the latest timestamp, a small `backtrack_minutes` won't re-fetch them.

**Fix:**

- Confirm there is genuinely new data: `pipe.get_sync_time()` shows the current upper bound.
- To force a full historical re-pull, sync with an explicit lower bound or no bound:

    ```bash
    mrsm sync pipes -c plugin:foo -m bar --begin 2020-01-01
    ```

    ```python
    pipe.sync(begin=None)   # no lower bound at all
    ```

- Widen the backtrack window so corrections are caught:

    ```python
    pipe.update_parameters({'fetch': {'backtrack_minutes': 1440}})  # re-fetch last 24h
    pipe.edit()
    ```

- To re-check and repair a historical range chunk-by-chunk, use [`verify`](pipes/syncing.md) instead of `sync`:

    ```bash
    mrsm verify pipes -c plugin:foo -m bar --begin 2024-01-01 --end 2025-01-01
    ```

See [Syncing](pipes/syncing.md) for the full fetch → enforce → filter → write flow.

---

### Duplicate rows appear

**Symptom:** The same logical record shows up multiple times in the target table.

**Cause:** Without a uniqueness definition, Meerschaum has no way to know two rows are "the same", so every sync appends. Uniqueness comes from the `datetime` and `id` index columns (and/or a `primary` column). If those aren't set, or if you want existing rows updated in place rather than appended, you need `upsert`.

**Fix:**

- Define index columns so rows can be deduplicated:

    ```python
    pipe.columns = {'datetime': 'timestamp', 'id': 'station_id'}
    pipe.edit()
    ```

- To update matching rows in place instead of inserting new ones, enable upsert:

    ```python
    pipe.upsert = True
    pipe.edit()
    ```

    This creates a unique index on the index columns and switches the write to an UPSERT.

---

### `Detected minimum datetime greater than maximum datetime.`

**Symptom:** This warning appears during a sync.

**Cause:** The incoming data's earliest timestamp is later than its latest, usually a malformed source query, a swapped `begin`/`end`, or mixed timezone parsing producing nonsensical ordering.

**Fix:** Inspect the fetched frame (`pipe.fetch(begin=..., end=...)`) and check the `datetime` column for parsing errors. Make sure `begin <= end` if you passed them explicitly.

---

## Datetimes & timezones

### Timezone-aware vs naive mismatch

**Symptom:** Rows silently fail to match on incremental syncs, comparisons behave oddly, or you see datetime cast warnings.

**Cause:** The pipe's `datetime` column is stored timezone-aware (`TIMESTAMPTZ` / UTC) by default, but the incoming data is naive (or vice versa). Mixing the two breaks window comparisons.

**Fix:**

- Check the column's timezone with `pipe.tzinfo` (returns `UTC`, `None`, etc.).
- Make incoming timestamps tz-aware (UTC is the convention), or explicitly opt into naive storage by registering the column dtype without a timezone. See the dtype list in [Parameters](pipes/parameters.md).

---

### `NaT` / nulls in the datetime axis

**Symptom:** Sync errors or rows dropped; the datetime axis has missing values.

**Cause:** The `datetime` index column drives the incremental sync window, null (`NaT`) values there have no defined position.

**Fix:** Clean the source so the datetime column is always populated, or move the nullable field out of the index. If you need nulls allowed in *other* index columns, set `null_indices: True` (see [Parameters](pipes/parameters.md)).

---

## Dtypes & schema

### `Detected different types for '<col>' (... vs ...), falling back to 'object'...`

**Symptom:** This warning during a sync, followed by the column being stored as a generic object/text type.

**Cause:** Incoming data for a column has a different type than what's already stored (e.g. ints one sync, strings the next). Meerschaum widens the column to `object` to avoid data loss.

**Fix:**

- Pin the column's dtype explicitly so incoming data is coerced consistently:

    ```python
    pipe.dtypes = {'reading': 'numeric'}   # or 'Int64', 'float64', etc.
    pipe.edit()
    ```

- Fix the source so the type is stable across syncs.

See the supported dtype strings in [Parameters](pipes/parameters.md).

---

### Column type changed after the first sync

**Symptom:** A column's database type isn't what you expected, or it changed on a later sync.

**Cause:** By default, Meerschaum auto-alters the schema, it adds new columns and widens types as incoming data evolves.

**Fix:**

- To **lock the schema** (no new columns, no alters), set `static: True`:

    ```python
    pipe.parameters['static'] = True
    pipe.edit()
    ```

- To pin individual column types, register them under `dtypes` (above) before the first sync.

---

### New column not added

**Symptom:** A field present in the incoming data never appears in the target table.

**Cause:** One of:

- `static: True`, schema changes are disabled entirely.
- `enforce: False`, dtype enforcement (which also captures new columns) is skipped, so untracked columns may be ignored.

**Fix:** Remove `static`/set it to `False` to allow auto-alter, and leave `enforce` at its default (`True`) unless you have a specific reason to skip enforcement. See [Parameters](pipes/parameters.md).

---

## Upserts & partitioned tables

### Upsert fails: `ON CONFLICT` has no matching unique constraint

**Symptom:** An upsert sync raises a database error complaining there is no unique/exclusion constraint matching the `ON CONFLICT` specification (PostgreSQL), or an equivalent error on MySQL/MSSQL.

**Cause:** On a **partitioned table** (a TimescaleDB hypertable *or* a native range-partitioned PostgreSQL / MySQL / MSSQL table, the default for datetime-axis pipes since v3.4.0), the partition column (your `datetime` column) is folded into the composite primary key. An upsert conflict target of the `primary` key alone therefore has no matching unique constraint, and the database rejects it. The conflict target **must include the datetime column** on partitioned tables.

**Fix:** Meerschaum handles this automatically, the conflict/join columns for a partitioned upsert are `[datetime_col, primary_key]`. If you hit this with a custom setup:

- Ensure your `columns['datetime']` is set so the partition column is known.
- Or opt the pipe out of native partitioning by setting `hypertable: False` before the table is created (only affects *newly* created tables, pre-existing plain tables aren't retroactively partitioned).

    ```python
    pipe.parameters['hypertable'] = False
    pipe.edit()
    ```

See the native-partitioning notes in [Maintenance](pipes/maintenance.md) and [Parameters](pipes/parameters.md).

---

## Connectors & instances

### `Unable to parse connector keys '<keys>'` / `Invalid connector keys`

**Symptom:** An action fails to resolve a connector.

**Cause:** Connector keys must be of the form `type:label` (e.g. `sql:main`, `api:mrsm`, `plugin:noaa`). A bare label, wrong type, or typo won't resolve.

**Fix:**

- List configured connectors: `mrsm show connectors`.
- Check the instance keys you're passing (`-i` / `--instance` / `mrsm_instance`) point at a real, configured instance.
- Add or edit a connector with `mrsm bootstrap connector` or by editing `MRSM_ROOT_DIR/config/connectors.yaml`.

---

### `Cannot create Connector of type '<type>'.`

**Symptom:** This warning when creating a connector.

**Cause:** The connector type isn't registered (no matching built-in or custom `@make_connector` class), or its config block is missing required attributes.

**Fix:** Verify the type is spelled correctly and that any custom connector plugin is installed/loaded. For SQL/API connectors you can supply config inline via a URI environment variable (next entry).

---

### Setting a connector via environment variable (URI)

**Symptom:** You want to point a connector at a database/API without editing config files.

**Cause:** N/A, this is the intended override mechanism.

**Fix:** Set `MRSM_SQL_<LABEL>` or `MRSM_API_<LABEL>` to a URI. The label becomes the connector's label (lowercased):

```bash
export MRSM_SQL_MAIN='postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/dbname'
export MRSM_API_MRSM='https://user:pass@api.example.com'
```

`MRSM_SQL_MAIN` above defines the `sql:main` connector. See [Environment](environment.md).

---

## API instances & auth

### Permission / authentication errors against an API instance

**Symptom:** Requests to an `api:` instance fail with `401`/`403`, "permission denied", or login failures.

**Cause:** The API connector has no valid credentials, the token/session expired, or the account lacks permission for the operation (e.g. registering pipes/plugins on a locked-down server).

**Fix:**

- Log in interactively: `mrsm login`, or bootstrap the connector with `mrsm bootstrap connector` to store credentials.
- Embed credentials in the URI (`MRSM_API_<LABEL>=https://user:pass@host`), see above.
- For non-interactive jobs, use an API token. See [API instance](api-instance/index.md).
- Confirm the server is reachable and the account has the needed role.

---

## Plugins

### Plugin dependencies fail to install / `ImportError` in a plugin

**Symptom:** A plugin errors on import, or its `required` packages aren't found at runtime.

**Cause:** Each plugin installs its dependencies into a **plugin-named virtual environment**. If `setup` hasn't run, or a dependency was added after install, the venv is stale.

**Fix:**

- Reinstall the plugin's dependencies:

    ```bash
    mrsm install plugin <name>   # or: mrsm setup plugins <name>
    ```

- Inside plugin/connector code, import heavy packages with `attempt_import(..., venv='<plugin_name>')` rather than a top-level import.

See [Plugins](plugins/index.md).

---

### Plugin changes not picked up

**Symptom:** You edited a plugin but Meerschaum runs the old code.

**Cause:** Plugins are cached in the running process / shell session.

**Fix:** Reload plugins (or restart the shell):

```bash
mrsm reload plugins
```

---

### Stale `~/.local` install shadows your working tree (developers)

**Symptom:** Running tests or `python -m meerschaum` reflects an *old* version (new modules are missing, behavior is outdated) even though your repo is up to date.

**Cause:** A separately installed `meerschaum` under `~/.local/lib/pythonX.Y/site-packages/` is earlier on `sys.path` than the repo checkout and shadows it.

**Fix:** `mrsm doctor` names the stale copy (`install: meerschaum package` reports its path). A Python worker (and the API host) also refuses to import a `meerschaum` of another major version, one that looks like v4, or one speaking another worker protocol (importing v4 would run its start-up, which installs packages whatever `MRSM_NO_AUTO_INSTALL` says), and says so once; for another release of the same major version it starts and warns once. Force the repo onto the path:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=$(pwd) python -m pytest ...
```

Verify with `import meerschaum; print(meerschaum.__file__, meerschaum.__version__)`. (The project's `scripts/test.sh` sets this up correctly.)

---

## Debugging tips

- **`--debug`**, add to any action to print resolved SQL, sync windows, and dtype enforcement. The single most useful diagnostic. See [Debug output](#debug-output) below for what it prints and where.

    ```bash
    mrsm sync pipes -c plugin:foo -m bar --debug
    ```

- **`mrsm show pipes`**, list the pipes matching your key filters; confirm the pipe exists and resolves to the instance you expect. Add `-i <instance>` to target a specific instance.

- **`pipe.get_sync_time()`**, the current upper bound of the datetime axis. If this is unexpectedly recent, your sync window is excluding older data.

    ```python
    import meerschaum as mrsm
    pipe = mrsm.Pipe('plugin:foo', 'bar')
    print(pipe.get_sync_time())
    ```

- **`pipe.parameters`**, inspect the full metadata dict: `columns`, `dtypes`, `fetch`, `upsert`, `static`, `enforce`, `hypertable`, etc. Most "why is it doing that?" questions are answered here.

    ```python
    import json
    print(json.dumps(pipe.parameters, indent=2, default=str))
    ```

- **`mrsm show columns` / `mrsm show rowcounts`**, confirm the stored schema and row counts match expectations.

- **`pipe.get_data(begin=..., end=..., params=...)`**, pull a sample directly to see what's actually stored.

### Debug output

`--debug` works on every action, and the shell's `debug on` toggle turns it on for every command
you type (and for the shell itself) until `debug off`. Each message starts with a header naming
the time (UTC) and the code that printed it, like v4's `dprint()`:

```text
 🐞 14:03:07.512 | meerschaum_cli::dispatch:935
Action ["sync", "pipes"] -> `sync pipes` (_sync_pipes), sub-actions [].
 🐞 14:03:07.519 | meerschaum_connector_sql::driver:707
SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type IN ('table', 'view') AND name = 'mrsm_pipes'
```

Rust code names its module (`meerschaum_connector_sql::driver`), Python code its module
(`meerschaum.connectors.sql._pipes`) or your plugin's. With `--debug` you see:

- the action the words resolved to and the parsed arguments. Secrets are printed as `***`:
  values of keys or flags named like `password`, `secret`, `token` or `api_key` (also inside
  `--params` and other JSON), URI passwords and secret query parameters (`?password=`);
- each connection opened (`sql:`, `api:` and `valkey:`: flavor, host, port, database, username;
  never the password);
- every SQL statement the native SQL connector runs (with the number of bound parameters);
- the sync stages with row counts and timings: fetch (each fetched chunk with its bounds, for
  chunked and generator sources too), dtype enforcement, the filter against existing rows
  (unseen vs. updated) and the write;
- the Syncing Engine's plan (action, reason, bounds and chunks per pipe) and each event as the
  run reaches it: nodes starting and finishing, every chunk with its bounds, row counts and
  duration;
- each call to a Python worker (operation, payload size, duration). `--debug` is forwarded to
  the worker, so `debug=True` reaches your plugin's `fetch()` / `sync()` / actions and their
  `dprint()` output appears too;
- plugin discovery and loading (native plugins, and Python plugins when the plugin manifest is
  rebuilt).

While a full-screen view (`watch run`, `watch jobs`, the shell's F2 / F3) is shown, debug output
is held back and printed when you leave the view (the last 2000 messages). `mrsm --debug` (or
`mrsm --shell --debug`) starts the shell with `debug` on; `debug off` turns it off.

Debug output goes to **stderr**, never stdout, so `mrsm ... --debug > out.txt` keeps the command's
real output clean, and job logs (which capture both streams) include it. In v5 Python's
`meerschaum.utils.debug.dprint()` also prints to stderr (v4 printed to stdout). The header is
colored with `formatting:debug` (`mrsm edit config`) when the output is styled (see
[Colors and Plain Output](/reference/actions/#colors-and-plain-output)); `formatting:ansi: false`
or `NO_COLOR` removes the colors and `formatting:unicode: false` replaces the icon with `DEBUG`.

From Python, `debug=True` on a pipe or connector method of a SQL instance (`pipe.sync(debug=True)`,
`pipe.get_data(debug=True)`, `pipe.clear(debug=True)`, `mrsm.get_pipes(debug=True)`, ...) shows
the Rust core's debug output for that call through `dprint()`. For any other call, wrap it in
`meerschaum._core.debugging()`:

```python
import meerschaum as mrsm
from meerschaum._core import debugging

with debugging():
    print(mrsm.Pipe('sql:main', 'demo').exists())
```

Debug output is on for the whole process while any `--debug` action, `debug=True` call or
`debugging()` block runs, so work running at the same time in other threads prints too. The API
server is the exception: an action a client runs with `debug` passes `debug=True` to the action
but does not turn on debug output for the server's other requests.

`RUST_LOG` is unrelated to `--debug`: it still prints the Rust `tracing` events its filter selects
(dependencies included) in the `tracing` format, for developers.

# ⬆️ Migrating to v5

Source: https://meerschaum.io/reference/migrating-to-v5/

# ⬆️ Migrating to v5

Meerschaum v5 runs its core, CLI, jobs, Compose, HTTP API, and MCP server in Rust. Your existing data, configuration, Pipe definitions, and Python plugins remain usable. Review the changes below before upgrading a shared installation.

## Upgrade checklist

1. Back up your configuration and database. Keep the old installation available for rollback.
2. Check Python **3.11+** and the [platform requirements](#installing-and-running).
3. Install the optional packages your plugins and DataFrame code use.
4. Review [permissions](#teams-access-and-permissions), especially accounts that run remote actions.
5. Test one source sync, one transformation, and your scheduled jobs on a copy of the root.
6. Check saved Job commands with `mrsm show jobs`. Re-enter a blank command with `mrsm edit jobs NAME` before restarting it.
7. Upgrade the owning installation and restart running services. For Docker, replace the image.

```bash
python -m pip install --upgrade meerschaum
mrsm doctor
```

See [Stack upgrades](stack/upgrades.md) for PostgreSQL and extension maintenance. Expand only the sections which apply to your installation.

## 🧭 Who needs to read what

| You... | Read |
|---|---|
| Run `mrsm` on a server, in Docker, or with compose, and only use built-in connectors | [Installing](#installing-and-running), [Configuration](#configuration), [Jobs and the CLI](#jobs-and-the-cli), [Deployment](#deployment), [Behavior changes](#behavior-changes-at-a-glance) |
| Write fetch / sync / action plugins, custom connectors, or hooks | The above, plus [Python library users](#python-library-users-and-scripts) and [Plugin authors](#plugin-authors) |
| Write `@api_plugin` routes or MCP tools | The above, plus [API plugins](#api-plugins) |
| Write `@dash_plugin` / `@web_page` pages | The above, plus [Web pages and Dash plugins](#web-pages-and-dash-plugins) |
| Want to write plugins in Rust | [Rust plugins](#rust-plugins) |
| Want to see what is new | [New in 5.0](#new-in-50) |

## ✅ What does not change

- **Your data and Pipe definitions.** Existing tables, keys, parameters, SQL templates, and dependencies remain usable.
- **Your configuration.** Keep `MRSM_ROOT_DIR`, YAML files, environment connectors, Compose projects, and plugin registrations.
- **Everyday commands.** `sync`, jobs, schedules, and the Python Pipe API keep their familiar interfaces.
- **Python extensions.** Fetch, sync, action, connector, API, and Dash plugins continue through the Python host.

Some defaults, errors, and permissions deliberately change. The next section lists those differences.

## ⚠️ Behavior changes at a glance

Use this table to check differences in errors, defaults, permissions, jobs, and SQL behavior.

<details markdown="1">
<summary>Compare behavior by area</summary>

Everything below is deliberate, and each item links to the section with the details. Check the ones that apply to you before upgrading.

| Area | v4.1 | v5 |
|---|---|---|
| `MRSM_NO_AUTO_INSTALL=1` | Stopped `attempt_import` from installing, but v4 still downloaded `semver` and the API imported `uv` at startup | Disables **every** implicit install, including the dependency prechecks. Installs you ask for (`install packages`, `pip_install(...)`) still run. [Details](#dependencies-and-venvs) |
| YAML tags | `!!python/object`, `/apply`, `/name`, ... in a config file or a pipe's parameters were constructed (they can import modules and call functions) | Refused with a `could not determine a constructor for the tag` error, exactly like `yaml.safe_load`. Only `!!python/tuple` (what Meerschaum itself writes) is read. [Configuration](#configuration) |
| Web console | A Plotly Dash app in the FastAPI server | The same app, served by the Python API host and proxied by the Rust server; the standalone binary shows a pointer page at `/dash`. [Web pages](#web-pages-and-dash-plugins) |
| Web terminal | A Tornado process; any logged-in user got a shell unless `api.permissions.actions.non_admin` was false or the server ran with `--secure` | Served by the API server and requires `webterm:use` (Operator or admin by default); the default Editor role has no terminal. `--secure` restricts it to administrators. The websocket refuses a cross-origin `Origin`, a second login works and the shell echoes. [Deployment](#deployment) |
| Plugin archives | Symlink and hard-link members were extracted | Refused (`Links are not allowed in plugin archives`); members are written under the target directory only, with a size cap. Plugin and venv names are one plain path component. [Deployment](#deployment) |
| `pipe.sync()` | A plain `(bool, str)` tuple | A `SyncResult` that unpacks like one and carries `inserted`, `updated`, `duration`, ... [Python users](#python-library-users-and-scripts) |
| Dask | `get_data(as_dask=True)` and syncing a Dask DataFrame | Raise a `TypeError` naming this guide. Use `as_iterator=True` or `as_polars=True`; pass `ddf.compute()` or a generator of chunks to `sync()`. [Python users](#python-library-users-and-scripts) |
| Config, `MRSM{}`, `{{ Pipe() }}` | Python | Rust. The files, keys and substitution are unchanged, and `get_config` still returns live dictionaries. Config YAML holding dates, bytes or very large integers now loads and writes back unchanged. [Python users](#python-library-users-and-scripts) |
| Writing a config file | Truncated the file, then wrote it | Writes a temporary file and renames it over the target, so a failed write never loses your connector passwords. A new config file is created `0600`. [Configuration](#configuration) |
| Job names, remote job environment, systemd units | See v4 | Stricter names, the server's environment, a pinned `MRSM_PYTHON`. [Jobs and the CLI](#jobs-and-the-cli) |
| CLI daemons | `start|stop|restart|show daemons` managed a warm interpreter | There is nothing to keep warm: `show daemons` reports none and `start daemons` / `start worker` explain that actions run natively. [Deployment](#deployment) |
| Editors | `$EDITOR`, else installed `pyvim` | `$VISUAL`, else `$EDITOR`, else `vi`. Nothing is installed to open an editor. [Deployment](#deployment) |
| Scopes | `*` entered in `edit tokens` / `edit users` was expanded to the built-in scope list; stopping a job over the API required the misspelled scope `josb:stop`; any user could register a token with any scopes, `*` included | `*` is stored literally and grants every scope, custom and future ones included; `POST /jobs/{name}/stop` requires `jobs:stop` (a token that holds the legacy `josb:stop` is still accepted); **a token carries at most its owner's scopes** (asking for more is refused with a `403` naming them), and only a token's owner or an administrator may edit, invalidate or delete it (only an administrator may make an invalidated token valid again). [Tokens](/reference/api-instance/tokens/#scopes) |
| `sql <label>` | Passed the connection URL with the password to `pgcli` / `mycli` | Prefers installed Rainfrog for supported flavors; keeps Python/plain fallbacks and configurable preferences. Credentials travel through the child environment, outside argv. `--nopretty` forces the plain client. |
| `sql <label> "<query>"` | The query went to the driver in one call: SQLite (`sqlite3`) and MySQL / MariaDB (`pymysql`) refused a string holding several statements (`a; b`) with a driver error and ran none of them | The text is sent as written, so `CREATE TABLE t (a INT); INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES (5)` runs on SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB like it already did on PostgreSQL and MSSQL (Oracle still takes one statement per call). Only SQL you type is affected |
| `sql <label> "<query>"` that contains `select` but changes data | v4 sends any text containing `select` through `read()`, which fails after the statement ran and, on most flavors, rolled it back silently: `INSERT ... SELECT` kept its rows only on MSSQL, and `CREATE VIEW ... AS SELECT` was kept on MSSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle and SQLite but not on PostgreSQL or DuckDB | The statement runs and is **committed** on every flavor, and the action still prints `None` after "This result object does not return rows" (DuckDB prints its `Count` table). |
| DuckDB | The Python `duckdb` package | Python hosts share the optional Python driver between Pipe operations and SQLAlchemy. Standalone and base-only installs load `libduckdb` at run time, downloading it when needed. Explicit `MRSM_DUCKDB_LIB` selects the native C API and refuses mixed SQLAlchemy access. [Installing and running](#installing-and-running) |
| Time zone objects | `ZoneInfo('Etc/UTC')` from psycopg | `datetime.timezone.utc` (equal values). [Python users](#python-library-users-and-scripts) |
| An unreachable database, API or Valkey server | The first query waited for the driver's own timeouts (30 s of retries for a refused PostgreSQL / MySQL connection, minutes for a host that never answers) | The first connection of a command fails at once with `sql:main: cannot connect to localhost:5432 (connection refused). Is the database running?` (also unknown host, rejected credentials), and a host that does not answer fails after `connect_timeout` (5 s). [Configuration](#configuration) |
| `--debug` and `dprint()` | `dprint()` printed to stdout; `--debug` showed the Python code's messages | Debug output goes to **stderr** (Python's `dprint()` too), so redirected output stays clean; job logs still include it. `--debug` and the shell's `debug on` also show the Rust core's messages (dispatch, connections, every SQL statement, sync stages, engine plans and chunks, worker calls, plugin loading) in the same format, with secrets redacted. [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#debug-output) |
| `MRSM_<TYPE>_<LABEL>` variables of an unknown type | Every such variable became a connector (`MRSM_DUCKDB_LIB` became `duckdb:lib`) | Ignored: only the built-in connector types and the types your plugins register are read. [Configuration](#configuration) |
| Registering a pipe, user or plugin twice | `mrsm_pipes`, `mrsm_users` and `mrsm_plugins` had no unique keys: two processes registering the same pipe, username or plugin at once could both insert a row (on Valkey, a second registration overwrote the user's password) | The first time 5.0 registers, syncs, edits or looks up a pipe or user, it adds the unique indexes `uq_mrsm_pipes_keys` (connector, metric and location keys; a missing location key counts as one, except on MySQL 5.7 and MariaDB) `uq_mrsm_users_username` and `uq_mrsm_plugins_plugin_name` (constraints on Oracle), and the second registration gets "is already registered." / "already exists." (a plugin is updated instead). If a pipe, username or plugin is already registered twice, nothing is deleted and that index waits until you remove the extra rows: `mrsm doctor` lists them and the `DELETE` that removes them. v4.1 works with the indexes. Valkey instances register pipes and users atomically. |
| Changing a pipe's `columns` | Not tracked | A changed `datetime` / `id` / `primary` column is a definition change: an engine run marks the pipe for `rebuild`. [The Syncing Engine](#the-syncing-engine) |
| Database errors in Python | `SQLConnector.read()` / `exec()` / `value()` and `pipe.get_data()` / `get_rowcount()` / `get_sync_time()` warned and returned `None` or `0`, so an outage looked like an empty pipe | They raise the database's error (on `api:` instances: an unreachable server or a `5xx` answer). `silent=True` keeps 4.1's results; a pipe that was never synced still reads as empty. [Python users](#python-library-users-and-scripts) |
| `'None'`, `'NA'`, `'nan'`, `''` and the other null-like strings | Written as `NULL`, and matched as `IS NULL` in `params` | In declared text columns and text index columns they are text, written and matched as such; only real nulls are `NULL`. Other columns, and `''` on Oracle, keep 4.1's rule. [Python users](#python-library-users-and-scripts) |
| Colors | Output stayed colored when piped or redirected | Styled only on a terminal; `NO_COLOR` turns styles off everywhere and `FORCE_COLOR` forces them. Jobs keep their colors. [Jobs and the CLI](#jobs-and-the-cli) |
| `mrsm -h`, `mrsm help` | argparse's page; `mrsm help` ran your shell's `help` builtin | Grouped actions first, then the options. Every option string, arity and type is unchanged. [Jobs and the CLI](#jobs-and-the-cli) |
| `start pipeline` | The serialized form of an action chain (`start pipeline <flags> -P {...}`) | Starts a saved Pipeline's background job. Chains keep their `+` / `:` syntax, and jobs stored in 4.1's form keep running. [Jobs and the CLI](#jobs-and-the-cli) |
| Executor of a non-default root | `local` | `systemd` on a systemd host, in every root; a root's `local` jobs move on its next `compose up` or `restart jobs`. [Jobs and the CLI](#jobs-and-the-cli) |
| `copy pipes` | Succeeded when any one pipe was copied | Fails (exit `1`) when any pipe fails, with a line per pipe. [Jobs and the CLI](#jobs-and-the-cli) |
| `mrsm python script.py ...` | Ran `script.py` as a line of code in the REPL | Runs the file; every word after its name is the script's. [Jobs and the CLI](#jobs-and-the-cli) |
| Pipes with the connector keys `mrsm` | Listed with your pipes | Hidden from listings and bulk actions unless you name them with `-c mrsm`. [Python users](#python-library-users-and-scripts) |
| `/dash` | The dashboard (key filters, command builder, web terminal) | The Overview. The dashboard is the Terminal page at `/dash/terminal`, and `/dash?action=...` links open it. [Web pages](#web-pages-and-dash-plugins) |
| Console callbacks | Answered any request | Need a console session, except the login and registration forms and the callbacks a plugin marks public. [Web pages](#web-pages-and-dash-plugins) |
| A user's scopes that cannot be read | A failed read granted every scope | The login or request is refused (`503`); Valkey's user reads raise `ConnectionError`. [Permissions](/reference/api-instance/permissions/#permissions-fail-closed) |
| `start api --keyfile/--certfile` | HTTPS through Uvicorn | Native HTTPS with rustls when a key and certificate are supplied; plain HTTP otherwise. [Deployment](#deployment) |
| Web terminal and tmux | Sessions on your default tmux server | A tmux server of its own under the Meerschaum root, with its own configuration. [Deployment](#deployment) |

</details>

## 📦 Installing and running

Use Python 3.11 or newer. Install `meerschaum[dash]` for the console, `meerschaum[pandas]` or `[polars]` for your DataFrame library, and your plugins' declared dependencies.

<details markdown="1">
<summary>Platform, installation ownership, and optional dependencies</summary>

- **Python 3.11 or newer** (only needed when you use Python plugins, the Python API or an extra). 3.10 reaches end of life in October 2026 and is not supported by the v5 wheels.
- **`pip install meerschaum` still works** and is the only PyPI package. Its `mrsm` (and `meerschaum`) console script runs the native CLI from the wheel's extension, and `python -m meerschaum ...` runs the same code. `cargo install meerschaum` builds the same CLI as a standalone `mrsm` binary: both install Meerschaum, like `polars`. The console script pays for loading the extension: `mrsm show version` takes about 35 ms (the Python interpreter alone is 15 ms) against about 10 ms for the standalone binary (measured on a Linux x86_64 development machine with the release build). Jobs, `systemd` units and compose steps run `python -m meerschaum`, so they carry the same start-up cost per process.
- **The base wheel has no third-party dependencies.** It depends on nothing. Build tooling is maturin; `setup.py` is gone, so build from source with `pip install .` (maturin backend) or `maturin build`. v4.1 installed about 110 packages into the shared `mrsm` venv on first run (pandas, dask, SQLAlchemy, three PostgreSQL drivers, Dash and its component libraries, rich, FastAPI, and so on). v5's `meerschaum` wheel contains the Rust core and the Python SDK and pulls in nothing else. Everything heavier is an extra, imported only when used:

    | Extra | Installs | You need it when |
    |---|---|---|
    | `meerschaum[pandas]` | pandas, pyarrow | You retain `dataframe: pandas` on an upgraded root, request `as_pandas=True`, or work with pandas inputs. A missing library raises an `ImportError` naming the extra (or installs it into the `mrsm` venv when automatic installs are allowed). |
    | `meerschaum[polars]` | polars | You use the new-root default, `dataframe: polars`, `as_polars=True`, or Polars inputs |
    | `meerschaum[geo]` | shapely, pyproj, GeoPandas, geoarrow-types (GeoPolars when released) | You use Python geometry objects or request a GeoDataFrame; Polars reads can keep WKB geometry without GeoPandas |
    | `meerschaum[sql]` | SQLAlchemy, psycopg, PyMySQL | Explicit `conn.engine` access and caller-provided SQLAlchemy connections. Native reads, writes and pipe operations do **not** need it. |
    | `meerschaum[sql-mssql]`, `[sql-oracle]`, `[sql-duckdb]`, `[sql-cockroachdb]` | pyodbc; oracledb; duckdb + duckdb-engine; sqlalchemy-cockroachdb | Explicit SQLAlchemy access against those flavors; `[sql-duckdb]` also provides DuckDB's optional shared Python transport. Native raw SQL does not require these extras. |
    | `meerschaum[api]` | FastAPI, uvicorn, a2wsgi, python-multipart, PyJWT, websockets | Any installed plugin uses `@api_plugin`, `@web_page` or registers an MCP tool |
    | `meerschaum[dash]` | Dash, a2wsgi, dash-bootstrap-components, dash-extensions | You want the web console (`/dash`), or any installed plugin uses `@dash_plugin` or a Dash `@web_page`. Includes the `api` extra, dash-ace and pandas, so `pip install meerschaum[dash]` is a working console. The host builds the console's app with `dash_extensions.enrich.DashProxy` (`Trigger`, duplicate outputs, as in v4) when dash-extensions is importable |
    | `meerschaum[shell]` | ptpython | You use `mrsm python` |
    | `meerschaum[gui]` | pywebview | You use `mrsm start gui` |
    | `meerschaum[cli-tools]` | pgcli, mycli, litecli, gadwall | You use `mrsm sql` to open a database shell |
    | `meerschaum[full]` | `pandas`, `polars`, `geo`, `sql`, `api`, `dash`, `shell` | You want all the optional Python integrations; the root's `dataframe` setting still selects returned frames |

    The Docker image installs `meerschaum[full]`; a new `bmeares/meerschaum:slim` tag installs only the base wheel.

    **Gone from every extra** (they served code that is now Rust): `dask`, `partd`, `joblib`, `psycopg2-binary`, `asyncpg`, `databases`, `aiosqlite`, `aiomysql`, `GeoAlchemy2`, `rich`, `prompt-toolkit`, `pygments`, `tabulate`, `humanfriendly`, `python-daemon`, `dill`, `psutil`, `watchfiles`, `gunicorn`, `httpx`, `valkey`, `python-jose`, `fastapi-login`, `aiofiles`, `python-dotenv`, `envyaml`, `terminado`, `tornado`, `dash-daq`, `Flask-Compress`, `modin`, `cmd2`, `ruamel.yaml`. If your plugin imports one of these, declare it in `required` (see [Dependencies and venvs](#dependencies-and-venvs)).

- **DuckDB uses an optional Python driver or a native library.** In Python, install `meerschaum[sql-duckdb]` and leave `MRSM_DUCKDB_LIB` unset so Pipe operations and SQLAlchemy share one driver. The standalone binary and base-only Python installs use DuckDB's own shared library, `libduckdb` (v1.5.6, MIT, published by the DuckDB project; Meerschaum does not redistribute it). When no cached or system library is available, the first native connection downloads the release asset for your platform (about 41 MB) into `MRSM_ROOT_DIR/drivers/duckdb/<version>/`, after checking it against a SHA-256 pinned in Meerschaum. Later native runs reuse it. `mrsm install driver duckdb` does the download on purpose (`--force` repeats it), `mrsm uninstall driver duckdb` removes it, and `mrsm show drivers` reports each driver's version, source (`env`, `cache`, `system` or `missing`) and path. **Behind a TLS-intercepting proxy** the download trusts the operating system's certificate store as well as its bundled roots, and honors `HTTPS_PROXY`; if it still cannot reach GitHub, run `mrsm install driver duckdb` on a machine that can and copy the library. **Air-gapped hosts:** copy a DuckDB library (v1.4 or newer) there and set `MRSM_DUCKDB_LIB` to its path, or put it on the system library path; `MRSM_NO_AUTO_INSTALL=1` forbids the implicit download and a missing library then fails with a message naming both fixes. In Docker, `--build-arg duckdb_driver=1` bakes it into the image's root. On Linux the library needs the C++ runtime (`libstdc++`), which both Docker images ship. Native Pipe sessions run in UTC (the official build bundles ICU, whose default is the host's zone), aware timestamp parameters keep their instant, and nested, interval and enum values read as the text DuckDB prints.
- **No Python at all** is an option: `cargo install meerschaum --locked` (Rust 1.95 or newer) or a release binary runs without an interpreter as long as no Python plugin, custom Python connector, API plugin or Dash plugin is used. Point `MRSM_PYTHON` at an interpreter when you add one.
- **Windows limits.** The Python API host is reached over loopback TCP with a per-start token on Windows (a Unix socket elsewhere), so `@api_plugin` routes, the Dash console and plugin pages work. Background jobs (`-d`), including Pipe management and Pipeline workers, are still refused; run those in Docker or WSL. Dashboard Exec submits into the existing terminal and does not require a background job.
- **Removed:** `pyoxidizer` builds and the standalone "portable" archive. `pip install meerschaum` and the standalone binary (`cargo install meerschaum`, release archives) replace them.

### Upgrading an installation

`mrsm upgrade mrsm` upgrades the installation providing the running engine. The planner
selects one published GitHub release and installs that exact release through the owning
backend: Python's environment installer (or its uv/pipx tool manager), Cargo using its
recorded install root, or checksum-verified replacement of a downloaded executable.
`mrsm doctor` reports the upgrade owner. Standalone development binaries and system-managed binaries
report the appropriate rebuild or package-manager instructions.

A stable install selects stable releases; an install of a pre-release keeps accepting
pre-releases. Use `mrsm upgrade mrsm -A --pre` to opt into pre-releases from a stable install, or
`mrsm upgrade mrsm -A --version 5.0.1` to select an exact release. An intentional
downgrade requires `--force`. Sub-arguments after `-A` that are not release options go to
the selected installer; a downloaded binary has no installer arguments.

`MRSM_PYTHON` chooses the optional Python extension host, never the self-upgrade destination.
When a distinct host is explicitly selected, the wizard offers to align its Meerschaum
package with the planned release. The default is no; `--yes` does not opt a separate host
in. An incompatible selected host must be aligned or changed before upgrading. Passing
Python extras (for example `upgrade mrsm full`) explicitly requests their installation in
the owning Python environment or the selected host. Native-only upgrades neither create
nor require a Python environment. Existing compatible user environments stay independently
managed. Installer failures are reported, including partial completion if a coordinated
host update succeeded before a CLI update failed.

After verification, an interactive shell restarts with the updated engine. Other running
processes must be restarted separately. Containers are upgraded by replacing their image;
see [Docker variants](stack/index.md#docker-images).

</details>

## ⚙️ Configuration

The existing YAML layout and environment connectors remain. Safe YAML loading, connection timeouts, and recognized connector types have stricter behavior.

<details markdown="1">
<summary>Configuration compatibility details</summary>

Everything under `MRSM_ROOT_DIR/config/` is read unchanged. Things to know:

- `api.uvicorn.*` keys (such as `forwarded_allow_ips`) are honored with a deprecation notice and mapped to `api.server.*`. Rename them at your leisure.
- **YAML is parsed by Meerschaum's own codec.** It reads and writes what v4 (PyYAML) did, byte for byte on the files Meerschaum writes, and keeps dates, bytes and very large integers intact. The one deliberate difference: the full-`Loader` tags `!!python/object`, `!!python/apply`, `!!python/name`, `!!python/module` and friends are **refused** like `safe_load` does, so a config file or a pipe's `parameters` can never run code. `!!python/tuple` is still read. A lone surrogate escape (`"\ud800"`) loads as U+FFFD.
- **Config files are written atomically.** `edit config`, `write_config` and the actions that save configuration write a temporary file in the same directory and rename it over the target, keeping its mode, owner and group (a new file is `0600`). A failed write never deletes or truncates the existing file. On a single bind-mounted file (`/meerschaum/config/plugins.json` in Docker) or a writable file in a read-only directory, the write falls back to rewriting the file in place, as v4 did.
- **Default pipe configuration may appear on startup.** Most v5 commands load the pipe defaults and can create `config/pipes.json` when it is missing. This file contains configuration defaults; registered pipes remain in their instance database. `mrsm doctor` uses read-only configuration and does not create it.
- **New:** `api.permissions.rate_limits`, keyed by route group (or a path prefix such as `/my-plugin` for a plugin's routes), so you no longer need HTTP middleware to throttle `/login` (see [API plugins](#api-plugins) and [Permissions and Rate Limits](/reference/api-instance/permissions/#rate-limits)):

    ```yaml
    api:
      permissions:
        rate_limits:
          login: {requests: 10, seconds: 60}
    ```

    `{max, window_seconds}` is accepted as the same. An entry the server cannot use (a count below 1, a window that is not a positive number, an unknown key, a name that matches no route group) is reported at startup.

- **New:** `api.permissions.preset: public` (or `mrsm start api --public`) serves only `/login`, `/healthcheck`, `/version`, plugin routes and plugin pages, for an API that exists to serve a plugin's public pages; route groups you allowlist are served on top. See [The public preset](/reference/api-instance/permissions/#the-public-preset).
- **New:** `protected: true` on a connector (or `?protected=true` on its URI) makes Meerschaum refuse every change through it until you pass `--allow-protected`, set `MRSM_ALLOW_PROTECTED=1` or use `meerschaum.connectors.allow_protected()`; reads are never blocked. `protected` is therefore a reserved connector attribute: a connector that used an attribute of that name for something else gets this behavior. See [Protected Connectors](/reference/connectors/#protected-connectors).
- **New:** `api.dash.callbacks_require_session` (default `true`; see [Web pages](#web-pages-and-dash-plugins)) and `api.webterm.tmux.config`, a tmux configuration file of yours for the web terminal's own tmux server (see [Deployment](#deployment)). `api.cache.connector` (default `valkey:main`) also backs the plugin SDK's [cache helper](/reference/plugins/caching/).
- **`meerschaum.executor: local`** in a root's config (or a Compose project's `config:`) keeps that root's jobs `local` now that every root defaults to `systemd` on a systemd host (see [Jobs and the CLI](#jobs-and-the-cli)).
- **Unknown `MRSM_<TYPE>_<LABEL>` variables are ignored.** v4 turned every such variable into a connector (`MRSM_DUCKDB_LIB` became a `duckdb:lib` connector). v5 reads a variable only when `<TYPE>` is a connector type that exists: `sql`, `api`, `valkey`, `plugin`, `systemd`, or a type one of your plugins registers with `@make_connector`. Everything else is skipped (a debug message names it).
- **Connections fail fast.** The first connection a command makes to a SQL, API or Valkey server reports a refused connection, an unresolvable host or rejected credentials immediately, and a host that does not answer fails after `connect_timeout` seconds (a connector attribute, or `MRSM_CONNECT_TIMEOUT` for every connector; 5 by default). A job that loses a connection it had established keeps v4's retry behavior. Serverless or auto-resuming databases (Azure SQL serverless, Neon, Aurora Serverless) can take 15 to 60 seconds to wake: raise `connect_timeout` for those connectors, and note that a job started before its database is up now exits at once instead of retrying for 30 s, so give it `restart: always` (compose) or a systemd unit with `Restart=`. See [`MRSM_CONNECT_TIMEOUT`](/reference/environment/#mrsm_connect_timeout).
- **New:** `system.engine.*` keys for the [Syncing Engine](#the-syncing-engine) (`workers`, `python_workers`, `limits.connectors`, `limits.instances`, `auto_rebuild`, `implicit_edges`, `inclusive_cap`, `flat_ledger`, `events`, `state_flush_ms`, `run_history_days`, `debounce_seconds`, `chunk_pipelining`, `default_duration_seconds`). All have defaults; you do not need to set any of them. The full table is in [Engine State](/reference/pipelines/state/#settings).

Run `mrsm show config` on v5 against a v4.1 root directory to see the resolved config.

</details>

## 🏃 Jobs and the CLI

Existing jobs are discovered in the same root. Installed systemd hosts now use systemd for every root; debug logs go to stderr and piped output omits terminal styles.

<details markdown="1">
<summary>CLI and job changes</summary>

Core actions behave the same and take the same flags: every option string, `dest`, arity, type and choice is diffed against the 4.1 parser in CI, argument for argument. The help text is new: `mrsm help`, `mrsm -h`, `mrsm show help` and the shell's `help` start with every action in groups (Create, Sync, Run, Inspect, Maintain, Configure) with a one-line description, then your plugins' actions and their subcommands, then the options (the graph-run flags under **Pipeline options**). Scripts that compared `mrsm -h` with 4.1's page byte for byte need updating, and `mrsm help` prints this page instead of running your shell's `help` builtin (`bash -c help` runs that one). `mrsm show data --gui`, `--trace`, `--cache`, `--no-daemon`, `--webterm-port`, `--use-bash` and `--allow-shell-job` are accepted and have no effect, and their help says so.

**Removed or renamed:**

| v4.1 | v5 |
|---|---|
| `--engine laps` | Gone. `--loop` is the only long-running mode and reproduces lap behavior (below). |
| `mrsm install plugin compose` | A no-op with a notice. Compose has been built in since 4.0. |
| A switch to "use the Python core" | Does not exist in 5.0. There is one core, and it is Rust. |
| `start pipeline <flags> -P '{"sub_args_line": ...}'` (how 4.1 stored an action chain) | Still runs, and jobs stored that way keep running. Write the chain as `a + b : <flags>`; `start pipeline NAME` now starts a saved Pipeline's background job (below). |
| `start api --keyfile ... --certfile ...` (HTTPS through Uvicorn) | Native HTTPS with rustls when a key and certificate are supplied; plain HTTP otherwise. [Deployment](#deployment) |

**Job executors (`systemd`, `api:<label>`) in 5.0.** Three behaviors differ from 4.1, all deliberate:

- **Job names are one path component.** `.`, `..`, the empty name and names containing `/`, `\` or NUL are rejected (4.1 only banned `,;'"$#=*&!` + backtick + `~`). A name is a directory under `jobs/`, so `DELETE /jobs/..` would otherwise address the whole root.
- **The environment of a job created over the API is the server's.** As in 4.1, `POST /jobs/{name}` replaces whatever `properties.env` the client sent with the server's environment. The one exception is the Compose project stamp, which is kept so that projects sharing one remote executor still own their jobs (4.1 loses it). A client cannot set other environment variables of a remote job.
- **Systemd units pin the Python interpreter.** The unit runs the `mrsm` binary and carries `Environment=MRSM_PYTHON=<absolute path>`: the `MRSM_PYTHON` (else the first `python3` on `PATH`) of the process which created the job. Plugins run under that interpreter however the unit is started later. `systemctl --user stop` of a job asks it to stop once; it stops at its next checkpoint, as with a single Ctrl+C.

**Every root uses systemd.** 4.1 picked the `systemd` executor only for the default root; other roots, Compose projects with their own `root_dir` included, ran `local` jobs that did not survive a reboot. On a systemd host an installed 5.0 picks `systemd` for every root. Units are named `mrsm-<job>.service` in the default root (as in 4.1), `mrsm-<project>.<job>.service` for a Compose project and `mrsm-<8 hex digits of the root's hash>.<job>.service` in any other root; they carry the root, the plugins directory and the project's environment, unit files are written `0600`, and each root lists only its own units (the default root no longer lists other roots' `mrsm-*.service`). A root's `local` jobs move to systemd on its next `compose up` or `restart jobs`: the old process is stopped first and its `logs/<job>.log.*` move to `systemd/logs/`. To keep a root's jobs local, set `meerschaum:executor: local` in its config (or the project's `config:`). A development build, a binary under a Cargo target directory and a package imported from a source checkout never pick `systemd` by themselves (`-e systemd` still works). Compose roots started from a system service or cron without a user bus need that setting too.

**`start pipeline` and action chains.** Commands joined with `+`, with flags for the whole chain after `:`, are called action chains; type them as before (`show version + show arguments : --loop`). A chain that runs as a job is stored under a hidden internal action, so `show jobs` prints it as you typed it, and jobs 4.1 stored as `start pipeline ... -P {...}` keep running unchanged. Chain messages say "action chain" instead of "pipeline" ("Ran the action chain 3 times.", "The action chain did not run.", "The action chain failed after 2 steps.", "Cancelled the action chain."), and `edit jobs` says "Chain Arguments:". `start pipeline NAME` / `stop pipeline NAME` (plurals and several names work) start and stop a saved Pipeline's background job: its scheduled job when it has one, else a new job `pipeline-NAME` running `sync pipelines NAME -i <instance> --loop --min-seconds 60`. `start pipeline` with neither a name nor a chain payload asks for a Pipeline's name (4.1 said "Nothing to do.").

**`--loop` works with any action, and jobs report their health.** `--loop` repeats any action `--min-seconds` apart (default 1), plugin actions included, retrying a failure after a pause that grows while it keeps failing (capped at an hour); `stop jobs` or Ctrl-C ends it after the current run. A plugin action whose function takes a `loop` parameter keeps 4.1's contract: `--loop` passes `loop=True` and the action repeats by itself. Every other action is repeated by Meerschaum and called once per run with `loop=False`. A job that repeats its work records each lap in `jobs/<name>/laps.json` (deleted with the job), and `show jobs`, `job.health` and the console report `healthy`, `failing`, `stalled` (no lap ended for three times the expected interval, at least a minute; an hour for `--listen`) or `stopped`. See [Job health](/reference/background-jobs/health/).

**`GET /jobs` redacts credentials, and the console's jobs are private.** 4.1 returned every job's `daemon.properties.env` (the server's environment when the job was created: each `MRSM_SQL_*` / `MRSM_API_*` connector URI with its password, and any other secret the process held) to every caller with `jobs:read`. 5.0 masks the password of connector URIs and the value of credential-named variables (`*_PASSWORD`, `*_TOKEN`, `*_SECRET*`, ...), also inside JSON values such as `MRSM_CONFIG`, in `GET /jobs` and `GET /jobs/{name}`; the other variables are unchanged. Automatic workers created by Pipe management and Pipeline runs are visible to their creator, their team’s managers and administrators only.
